stem: A student revises psychology in a silent library while a friend attempts to revise the same material while listening to music and checking messages. Which distinction best captures the difference in attentional demand between the two students?
why: The library student uses selective attention, focusing on revision while excluding irrelevant stimulation. The friend divides attention across revision, music and messages. Sustained attention concerns maintaining focus over time; alternating attention concerns switching between tasks.

optWhy.A: Correct: selective attention excludes distraction; divided attention shares capacity across tasks.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: sustained attention concerns duration over time, not exclusion of distraction.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: focused attention is a form of selective attention; involuntary attention is capture by a stimulus.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: both students are attending voluntarily; the key distinction is how attention is allocated.

stem: A driving instructor talks a learner through a manoeuvre while the learner simultaneously steers, checks mirrors and monitors speed. After several minutes the learner's steering becomes erratic. Which form of attention is most likely overloaded?
why: The learner must allocate limited attentional capacity across several concurrent tasks (steering, mirror checks, speed monitoring, verbal instruction). This is divided attention; capacity overload produces performance deterioration. Sustained attention is maintenance over time; alternating is switching between tasks.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: sustained attention concerns maintaining focus over a period, not concurrent task coordination.
optWhy.B: Correct: multiple simultaneous tasks impose divided-attention demands on limited capacity.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: alternating attention involves switching from one task to another, not doing several at once.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: involuntary attention is stimulus-driven capture, not the coordination required here.

stem: Match each attentional scenario to the form of attention it primarily illustrates.
listI: 1. Listening to a single speaker in a noisy room
2. Watching a clock for a rare signal over thirty minutes
3. Switching between writing a report and answering emails
4. A sudden loud bang captures a reader's attention
why: Listening to one speaker amid noise is selective attention (1-ii). Watching for a rare signal over time is sustained attention (2-i). Switching between report and emails is alternating attention (3-iv). A sudden loud bang capturing attention is involuntary attention (4-iii).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-ii, 2-i, 3-iv, 4-iii matches each scenario to its attentional form.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: scenario 1 is selective, not sustained; scenario 3 is alternating, not involuntary.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: scenario 2 is sustained, not involuntary; scenario 3 is alternating, not sustained.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: scenario 1 is selective attention, not involuntary attention.

key: Forms of attention matched to scenarios

stem: In a Broadbent-style dichotic-listening experiment, participants hear different digit sequences in each ear and are instructed to report all digits from one ear before the other. Participants typically report digits ear-by-ear rather than by serial position across ears. This result is taken to support:
why: Reporting digits ear-by-ear indicates a physical filter selects one channel for processing before semantic analysis; the unattended channel is blocked. This is the signature prediction of Broadbent's early-selection filter model. Attenuation and late-selection models would allow more semantic processing of the unattended channel.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: attenuation predicts weakened but not blocked processing of the unattended ear.
optWhy.B: Correct: ear-by-ear reporting supports an early physical filter selecting one channel.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: late selection analyses all inputs semantically before selecting, unlike the observed pattern.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Kahneman's model concerns allocation of effort, not ear-by-ear reporting in dichotic listening.

key: Broadbent filter model and dichotic listening

stem: In Broadbent's filter model of attention, the selective filter operates on the basis of:

options.text: The meaning of the incoming message
The emotional relevance of the message

why: Broadbent's filter is an early-selection filter that selects one channel based on physical characteristics (for example, which ear the message arrives in) before any semantic analysis. Meaning and emotional relevance are analysed only after the filter, in the limited-capacity channel.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: semantic analysis occurs after the filter, not at the filter stage.
optWhy.B: Correct: the filter selects by physical characteristics such as ear of input.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: emotional relevance is a semantic/meaning-based property, analysed post-filter.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: motivation influences capacity allocation (Kahneman), not Broadbent's physical filter.

stem: In a shadowing task, a participant repeats aloud a message presented to one ear while ignoring a message in the other ear. According to Broadbent's filter model, the unattended message:

options.text: Is analysed for meaning but not reported
Is blocked by the filter before semantic analysis
Is processed equally with the attended message
Receives full attention but is held in sensory memory

why: Broadbent's filter blocks the unattended channel before semantic analysis, so little or no meaning of the unattended message is extracted. This explains why shadowers typically report almost nothing about the unattended message except gross physical features.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: meaning analysis of the unattended channel is excluded by the early filter.
optWhy.B: Correct: the unattended channel is filtered out before semantic processing.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Broadbent's single-channel model does not process both messages equally.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: sensory memory is brief, and the unattended message is filtered, not fully attended.

key: Shadowing and the unattended channel under Broadbent

stem: Treisman's attenuation model differs from Broadbent's filter model in that Treisman proposes the unattended channel is:

options.text: Weakened but not eliminated, allowing some analysis
Analysed fully before any selection occurs
Stored in long-term memory for later retrieval

why: Treisman replaced Broadbent's all-or-none filter with an attenuator: the unattended channel is turned down rather than turned off, so highly salient or meaningful input (such as one's own name) can still break through.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: complete blocking is Broadbent's filter, not Treisman's attenuation.
optWhy.B: Correct: attenuation weakens the unattended channel without eliminating it.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: full analysis before selection describes late-selection models, not attenuation.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: long-term storage is not the mechanism by which unattended input breaks through.

stem: Match each phenomenon under the attenuation model to its explanation.
listI: 1. Hearing one's own name in the unattended channel
2. A low-threshold word breaks through attenuation
3. The attended channel is processed more fully
4. Semantic analysis of unattended input is partial
listII: i. Attenuation lowers the threshold for important words
ii. Dictionary units have different thresholds
iii. Attenuation is reduced for the attended message
iv. Attention determines which dictionary units are primed
why: One's own name has a low threshold and breaks through attenuation (1-ii). A low-threshold word breaks through because important words have low thresholds (2-i). The attended channel has reduced attenuation (3-iii). Unattended input receives only partial semantic analysis because attenuation limits processing (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-ii, 2-i, 3-iii, 4-iv matches Treisman's attenuation account.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: one's own name breaks through via low threshold (ii), not via the general low-threshold rule (i).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the attended channel is not matched to iii in the right way; own-name is ii.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 2-iv misassigns word breakthrough; the correct pairing is 2-i.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Treisman's attenuation model can explain why a participant notices their own name in the unattended auditory channel.
reason: Important words such as one's own name have low thresholds in the attenuation system.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: the cocktail-party / own-name phenomenon is explained by attenuation rather than complete filtering. The reason is true and correctly explains it: low-threshold dictionary units for salient items such as one's own name can break through the attenuated unattended channel.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and low thresholds explain breakthrough of the unattended name.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain why the name is noticed under attenuation.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

sub: Deutsch and Deutsch Late Selection Model
stem: In Deutsch and Deutsch's late-selection model of attention, selection occurs:

options.text: Before any semantic analysis of the input
After all inputs have been analysed for meaning
Only for the physically intense stimulus
At the sensory register, before perception

why: Deutsch and Deutsch proposed that all inputs are analysed semantically and that selection occurs late, close to the response stage, based on the importance of the input. This contrasts with Broadbent's early physical filter.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: pre-semantic selection is Broadbent's early filter, not late selection.
optWhy.B: Correct: all inputs receive semantic analysis before selection in the late-selection model.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: physical intensity is not the selection criterion in Deutsch and Deutsch's model.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: selection is not at the sensory register; it is late and response-related.

sub: Deutsch and Deutsch Late Selection Model
stem: Consider the following statements about early- and late-selection models of attention.
statements: 1. Broadbent's filter model selects one channel before semantic analysis.
2. Treisman's attenuation model blocks the unattended channel completely.
3. Deutsch and Deutsch's model analyses all inputs semantically before selection.
4. Late selection places the locus of selection closer to the response than early selection.
why: Statement 1 is correct: Broadbent selects before semantic analysis. Statement 2 is false: Treisman attenuates rather than completely blocks the unattended channel. Statement 3 is correct: Deutsch and Deutsch analyse all inputs semantically. Statement 4 is correct: late selection occurs closer to response than early selection. Therefore 1, 3 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 3 and 4 are true; statement 2 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.

stem: According to Johnston and Heinz's multimode model of attention, the point at which selection occurs (early or late) depends on:

options.text: The physical intensity of the stimuli alone
Whether the stimulus is attended or unattended

why: Johnston and Heinz proposed a flexible, multimode system in which selection can occur early or late depending on perceptual load and task demands. High load promotes early selection; low load permits later, more semantic processing.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: physical intensity alone does not determine the selection point in the multimode model.
optWhy.B: Correct: perceptual load and task demands determine early versus late selection.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: attended versus unattended is an outcome, not the determinant of selection point.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: long-term memory capacity is not the determinant of the selection locus.

stem: At a party, a person fails to follow most of the unattended conversation but immediately notices when someone says their name. This pattern is best explained by:

options.text: Treisman's attenuation with low-threshold dictionary units

why: Selective failure to process the unattended conversation with breakthrough of one's own name fits Treisman's attenuation model: the unattended channel is weakened, but low-threshold, personally significant units such as one's own name can still break through.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: Broadbent's complete filter would prevent any awareness of the name.
optWhy.B: Correct: attenuation plus low-threshold units explains selective processing with name breakthrough.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: late selection would process the unattended conversation semantically, not leave it largely unnoticed.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: capacity allocation explains effort distribution, not the specific name-breakthrough pattern.

key: Cocktail party / own-name effect under attenuation

stem: Consider the following statements about Broadbent's filter model.
statements: 1. The model assumes a single limited-capacity channel.
2. The filter selects input based on physical characteristics.
3. Semantic analysis occurs before the filter operates.
4. The unattended channel is completely blocked.
why: Statement 1 is correct: Broadbent's model has one limited-capacity channel. Statement 2 is correct: the filter selects by physical characteristics such as ear. Statement 3 is false: semantic analysis occurs after the filter. Statement 4 is correct in Broadbent's original formulation: the unattended channel is blocked. Therefore 1, 2 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 1 is also true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

sub: Deutsch and Deutsch Late Selection Model
stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Deutsch and Deutsch's late-selection model predicts that the unattended message in dichotic listening receives semantic analysis.
reason: Selection occurs only after all inputs have been analysed for their meaning.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: late selection holds that unattended input is analysed semantically. The reason is true and correctly explains it: selection occurs after semantic analysis of all inputs, so the unattended message is analysed before selection.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and post-semantic selection explains unattended semantic analysis.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

key: Late selection and semantic analysis of unattended input

stem: A proofreader checks a long document for spelling errors, then answers a phone call, then returns to proofreading. The proofreading requires sustained attention; the shift to the phone call and back requires alternating attention. If the proofreader instead tries to proofread while holding a conversation, which attentional form is primarily taxed?
why: Proofreading while conversing requires sharing attentional capacity between two concurrent tasks, which is divided attention. Alternating attention would be switching between them one at a time; sustained attention is maintaining proofreading over time.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: sustained attention is maintaining proofreading over time, not combining it with conversation.
optWhy.B: Correct: two concurrent tasks tax divided attention.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: alternating attention switches serially between tasks, not concurrent performance.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: involuntary attention is stimulus capture, not concurrent task coordination.

key: Divided attention in concurrent task performance

stem: Match each attentional model to its defining characteristic.
listII: i. All inputs analysed semantically; selection late
ii. Unattended channel weakened, not blocked
iii. Flexible early or late selection depending on load
iv. Early physical filter blocks unattended channel
why: Broadbent: early physical filter blocks unattended channel (1-iv). Treisman: unattended channel weakened, not blocked (2-ii). Deutsch and Deutsch: all inputs analysed semantically; selection late (3-i). Johnston and Heinz: flexible early or late selection depending on load (4-iii).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-iv, 2-ii, 3-i, 4-iii matches each model to its characteristic.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: Broadbent is not attenuation (ii); Treisman is not the physical filter (iv).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Treisman is weakened-not-blocked (ii), not all-inputs semantic analysis (i).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Broadbent is the physical filter (iv), not flexible selection (iii).

key: Models of attention matched to characteristics

stem: A driver notices a red traffic light without intending to look for it, having decided in advance to watch for signals. This combination of intention and stimulus-driven capture reflects:

options.text: Voluntary and involuntary attention acting together

why: The driver's decision to watch for signals is voluntary (endogenous) attention; the capture by the red light is involuntary (exogenous) attention. Both operate together in everyday attention.

optWhy.A: Correct: voluntary intention plus stimulus-driven capture are voluntary and involuntary attention.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: sustained attention concerns duration over time, not this combination.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: selective attention excludes distraction, whereas here the signal is the target.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: alternating attention switches between tasks, not intention plus capture.

stem: Consider the following statements about Treisman's attenuation model.
statements: 1. The unattended channel is completely blocked from semantic analysis.
2. Attenuation lowers the signal strength of the unattended message.
3. Low-threshold words can break through the unattended channel.
4. The model explains the own-name effect in dichotic listening.
why: Statement 1 is false: Treisman attenuates rather than completely blocks the unattended channel. Statement 2 is correct: attenuation reduces signal strength. Statement 3 is correct: low-threshold words such as one's own name break through. Statement 4 is correct: the model explains the own-name effect. Therefore 2, 3 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 2, 3 and 4 are true; statement 1 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 1 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 1 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 1 is false.

sub: Deutsch and Deutsch Late Selection Model
stem: An experiment shows that participants can classify the meaning of words in the unattended channel even while shadowing the attended channel, but only when the task is easy. This result most strongly supports:
why: Semantic processing of the unattended channel under easy-task conditions, with flexibility depending on task demands, supports Johnston and Heinz's multimode model: selection point shifts with perceptual load and task demands. Broadbent would not predict unattended semantic analysis at all.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: Broadbent's filter blocks unattended semantic analysis.
optWhy.B: Correct: flexible selection depending on task demands is the multimode model.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Kahneman's model concerns effort allocation, not the locus of selection.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Feature Integration Theory concerns visual feature binding, not auditory selection locus.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Broadbent's filter model cannot fully explain the cocktail-party effect (noticing one's own name in the unattended channel).
reason: The unattended channel is blocked before semantic analysis in Broadbent's model.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: the cocktail-party effect is a difficulty for Broadbent's model. The reason is true and correctly explains it: because Broadbent blocks the unattended channel before semantic analysis, it cannot account for meaningful unattended content such as one's own name breaking through.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and the pre-semantic block explains the model's difficulty with the effect.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

key: Cocktail-party effect limitation of filter model

stem: Match each form of attention to its definition.
listII: i. Maintaining attention on a task over a period of time
ii. Allocating attention to two or more tasks at once
iii. Concentrating on a single stimulus or task
why: Focused attention is concentration on a single stimulus or task (1-iii). Sustained attention is maintaining attention over time (2-i). Divided attention is allocating attention to two or more tasks at once (3-ii). Alternating attention is switching between tasks (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-iii, 2-i, 3-ii, 4-iv matches each form to its definition.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: sustained attention is not concentration on a single stimulus (that is focused attention).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: focused attention is not switching between tasks.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: divided attention is concurrent allocation, not concentration on a single stimulus.

stem: Consider the following statements comparing selection models of attention.
statements: 1. Early-selection models place the filter before semantic processing.
2. Late-selection models place the filter after semantic processing.
3. Treisman's attenuation is a form of early selection with an all-or-none filter.
4. The multimode model allows the selection point to vary with task demands.
why: Statement 1 is correct: early selection filters before semantic processing. Statement 2 is correct: late selection filters after semantic processing. Statement 3 is false: attenuation is not an all-or-none filter; it weakens rather than blocks. Statement 4 is correct: the multimode model varies the selection point with task demands. Therefore 1, 2 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: In a dichotic-listening experiment, participants shadow an attended message and rarely report the content of the unattended message, except when emotionally significant words appear. This selective breakthrough is best accommodated by:
why: Rare reporting of unattended content with breakthrough of emotionally significant words fits Treisman's attenuation model: the unattended channel is weakened but not blocked, and low-threshold significant items can break through.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: Broadbent's complete filter would prevent emotional-word breakthrough.
optWhy.B: Correct: attenuation plus low-threshold significant units explains selective breakthrough.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: late selection would process unattended content semantically, not leave it rarely reported.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the multimode model concerns the locus of selection, not this specific breakthrough pattern.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: The distinction between early and late selection concerns the stage at which the attentional filter operates.
reason: Early selection filters before semantic analysis, whereas late selection filters after semantic analysis.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: early versus late selection concerns the processing stage at which the filter operates. The reason is true and correctly explains it: early selection filters before semantic analysis; late selection filters after semantic analysis.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and the stage difference explains the early/late distinction.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

stem: According to Kahneman's capacity model of attention, attention is best understood as a:

options.text: limited pool of mental effort or capacity
filter that blocks all unattended input
process that operates without resource limits

why: Kahneman's capacity model treats attention as a limited pool of mental effort that can be allocated across tasks, governed by arousal and enduring dispositions. It is not a single sensory channel (Broadbent) nor an all-or-nothing filter.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: a single sensory channel describes Broadbent's filter model, not Kahneman's capacity model.
optWhy.B: Correct: attention is a limited pool of effort allocated according to arousal and dispositions.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: complete blocking of unattended input is Broadbent's filter, not Kahneman's model.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Kahneman explicitly proposes limited capacity, not unlimited processing.

stem: A student solves a complex maths problem while holding a conversation. As the maths problem becomes harder, the student's conversation becomes increasingly disjointed. Kahneman's model explains this as:

options.text: loss of a long-term memory trace

why: As the maths problem demands more capacity, less remains for conversation, so conversation deteriorates. This is competition for a single limited pool of attentional effort, the core claim of Kahneman's capacity model.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: sensory memory is brief and pre-attentive, not the resource being contested here.
optWhy.B: Correct: two concurrent tasks draw on one limited capacity pool; greater demand on one impairs the other.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: sensory transduction concerns receptor activation, not divided attention.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: long-term memory loss would not cause moment-to-moment conversational disjointedness.

key: Limited attentional capacity in dual-task performance

stem: Consider the following statements about Kahneman's capacity model of attention.
statements: 1. Kahneman's model views attention as a limited resource.
2. Allocation of effort is influenced by arousal.
3. The model requires a physical filter that blocks the unattended channel completely.
4. Enduring dispositions influence how capacity is allocated.
why: Statement 1 is correct: attention is a limited resource. Statement 2 is correct: arousal affects available capacity. Statement 3 is false: complete blocking of the unattended channel is Broadbent's filter model, not Kahneman's capacity model. Statement 4 is correct: enduring dispositions guide allocation. Therefore 1, 2 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false and statement 1 is also true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: In Treisman's Feature Integration Theory, the detection of a target defined by a conjunction of two features (for example, a red X among red Os and green Xs) requires:

options.text: focused, serial attention to bind features

why: A single feature pops out preattentively, but a conjunction of features requires focused attention to bind the features to one object, serial across items. Long-term memory and spontaneous recovery are unrelated to this binding mechanism.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: preattentive parallel processing detects single features, not conjunctions.
optWhy.B: Correct: conjunction targets require focused serial attention to bind features into objects.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: long-term memory retrieval is not the mechanism for visual feature binding.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: spontaneous recovery is a learning/conditioning phenomenon.

stem: In a visual search display, a red target pops out immediately among green distractors regardless of set size, but finding a red circle among red squares and green circles takes longer as distractors increase. This contrast demonstrates:
why: A target defined by one feature (red among green) pops out through preattentive parallel processing. A target defined by a conjunction (red circle) requires serial attention, so reaction time rises with set size.

optWhy.A: Correct: single-feature pop-out versus serial conjunction search.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: sensory adaptation is reduced responsiveness to unchanging stimulation.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: proactive interference is earlier learning disrupting later recall.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: echoic persistence concerns brief auditory sensory storage.

stem: In Treisman and Schmidt's illusory-conjunction experiment, briefly presented red circles and green triangles are sometimes reported as a red triangle that was never physically present. This occurs because:

options.text: features are bound correctly under all conditions
without focused attention, preattentively registered features recombine erroneously
the targets are stored in echoic memory

why: Features such as colour and shape are registered preattentively, but focused attention is required to bind them correctly. Without attention, free features recombine, producing an illusory conjunction such as a red triangle never presented.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: binding fails without attention, so features are not bound correctly.
optWhy.B: Correct: unattached features recombine into illusory objects without focused attention.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: echoic memory is auditory sensory storage, not visual feature binding.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: attentional capacity is limited, and the error is a binding failure.

key: Illusory conjunctions from failed feature binding

stem: Automatic processing is best distinguished from controlled processing by:

options.text: automatic requires conscious intention; controlled does not
automatic is fast, involuntary and consumes little capacity; controlled is slow, voluntary and capacity-demanding
automatic applies only to vision; controlled applies only to audition
automatic is always accurate; controlled is error-prone

why: Automatic processing is fast, involuntary and largely capacity-free (for example, reading a familiar word). Controlled processing is slow, voluntary and demands capacity (for example, naming an ink colour). The domains are not modality-specific, and neither is invariably accurate.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: this reverses the definitions; controlled processing is the intentional one.
optWhy.B: Correct: automatic is fast/involuntary/capacity-free; controlled is slow/voluntary/capacity-demanding.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: both automatic and controlled processing operate across sensory modalities.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: automatic processes can produce errors (for example, Stroop interference).

stem: A practised reader cannot avoid reading the meaning of a word even when instructed to name only its ink colour. This Stroop interference arises because:

options.text: word reading is automatic and colour naming is controlled
colour naming is automatic and word reading is controlled

why: Reading a familiar word is highly automatic and difficult to suppress, while naming ink colour is controlled and capacity-demanding. The automatic word reading interferes with the controlled colour-naming task, producing Stroop interference.

optWhy.A: Correct: automatic word reading intrudes on controlled colour naming.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: colour naming is controlled, not automatic, in practised readers.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: this reverses the automaticity of the two processes.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: sensory memory overload is not the mechanism of Stroop interference.

key: Stroop interference: automatic word reading vs controlled colour naming

stem: In a Stroop experiment, incongruent trials (for example, the word RED printed in green ink) produce slower colour-naming responses than congruent trials. This pattern indicates that:

options.text: reading the word is controlled and colour naming is automatic
automatic word reading interferes with controlled colour naming

why: The automatic tendency to read the word competes with the controlled task of naming the ink colour. On incongruent trials this competition slows responses; on congruent trials word and colour support the same response.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: reading is the automatic process, not colour naming.
optWhy.B: Correct: automatic word reading interferes with controlled colour naming.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: iconic memory decay is unrelated to Stroop colour-naming latency.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: proactive interference concerns prior learning disrupting recall, not this within-task conflict.

stem: A person fails to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through a basketball game while counting passes. This inattentional blindness demonstrates that:

options.text: unattended stimuli can be completely missed when attention is engaged elsewhere

why: When attention is engaged in a demanding task (counting passes), salient but unattended objects can go completely unnoticed. This shows that attention is selective and limited, not that all stimuli are registered.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: inattentional blindness shows attention is limited, not unlimited.
optWhy.B: Correct: engaging attention on one task can cause failure to notice an unexpected unattended object.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: echoic memory is auditory sensory storage and does not capture all events.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: sustained attention is not automatic; it is a form of selective attention over time.

stem: Consider the following statements about attentional limitations.
statements: 1. Inattentional blindness is failure to notice an unexpected object when attention is engaged.
2. Change blindness is failure to notice a change between two views of a scene.
3. Selective attention prevents all distraction from unattended stimuli.
4. Attentional capture can occur without conscious intent.
why: Statement 1 is correct: inattentional blindness is missing an unexpected object during an engaging task. Statement 2 is correct: change blindness is missing changes across views. Statement 3 is false: selective attention does not prevent all distraction (salient stimuli can capture attention). Statement 4 is correct: attentional capture can be involuntary. Therefore 1, 2 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

sub: Experimental Paradigms: Dichotic Listening and Shadowing
stem: Match each attentional paradigm or finding to the model or description it supports.
listII: ii. repeating the attended message aloud
iv. attending one channel at a time
why: Dichotic listening supports Broadbent's early selection (1-i). Shadowing is repeating the attended message aloud (2-ii). Hearing one's own name in the unattended channel is attenuation breakthrough (3-iii). Ear-by-ear reporting reflects attending one channel at a time (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-i, 2-ii, 3-iii, 4-iv matches each paradigm to its account.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: dichotic listening is not shadowing; shadowing is not early selection itself.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: own-name is attenuation (iii), not early selection (i).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: misassigns all four pairings.

key: Dichotic listening, shadowing and own-name effect

sub: Experimental Paradigms: Dichotic Listening and Shadowing
stem: In a shadowing task, the participant:

options.text: repeats the attended message aloud while ignoring the unattended message
detects all changes in the unattended channel

why: Shadowing requires the participant to vocalise the attended message in real time while disregarding the unattended channel. It is the standard procedure for studying selective auditory attention.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: shadowing requires actively attending to and repeating one message.
optWhy.B: Correct: shadowing is aloud repetition of the attended message with the unattended ignored.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: shadowing is online repetition, not delayed recall of both messages.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the unattended channel is largely not monitored in shadowing.

stem: Consider the following statements about attention experiments.
statements: 1. Stroop interference shows word reading is more automatic than colour naming.
2. Feature search is faster than conjunction search as set size increases.
3. Visual search pop-out requires focused serial attention for every item.
4. The Stroop effect is reduced when the task is to read the word rather than name the ink colour.
why: Statement 1 is correct: word reading is highly automatic and intrudes on colour naming. Statement 2 is correct: feature search is efficient (flat set-size function) whereas conjunction search is serial. Statement 3 is false: pop-out is preattentive and parallel, not focused serial attention for every item. Statement 4 is correct: reading the word is largely unaffected by ink colour because reading is automatic. Therefore 1, 2 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: A participant searches for a blue triangle among blue circles and green triangles. Reaction time increases steadily as more distractors are added. The target is defined by:

options.text: a conjunction of colour and shape requiring serial search

why: The target (blue triangle) shares colour with blue distractors and shape with green distractors, so it is defined by a conjunction of colour and shape. Conjunction targets require serial attention, so reaction time rises with set size.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: a single feature would pop out and show little set-size effect.
optWhy.B: Correct: blue triangle is a colour-shape conjunction requiring serial search.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: an echoic trace is auditory sensory storage, unrelated to visual search.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: a conditioned stimulus is a learning construct, not a visual-search target.

stem: The Gestalt approach to perception is best characterised by the claim that:

options.text: perception is the sum of independent sensations
the whole is other than the sum of its parts
perception depends only on retinal images

why: Gestalt psychology holds that perceptual wholes have properties not reducible to their component sensations ('the whole is other than the sum of its parts'). It opposes elementist/sensation-based accounts.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: summing independent sensations is the elementist/structuralist view, opposed by Gestalt.
optWhy.B: Correct: the whole has emergent properties beyond its parts, central to Gestalt.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Gestalt does not claim perception is entirely learned; organisation is innate.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Gestalt emphasises organisation beyond the retinal image.

key: Gestalt holism: whole is other than sum of parts

stem: Match each perceptual scenario to the Gestalt principle it illustrates.
listI: 1. Dots arranged in columns are perceived as columns because dots within each column are closer together
2. Two rows of dots, one row red and one row blue, are perceived as two colour groups
3. A circle with small gaps is perceived as a complete circle
4. Several dots move together in the same direction and are perceived as one group
why: Closer spacing within columns groups dots into columns: proximity (1-ii). Same colour groups the two rows: similarity (2-iii). Gaps are filled in to see a complete circle: closure (3-i). Common direction of movement groups the dots: common fate (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-ii, 2-iii, 3-i, 4-iv matches each scenario to its principle.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: scenario 1 is proximity, not closure.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: scenario 1 is proximity, not similarity.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: misassigns all four scenarios.

stem: Match each Gestalt principle to its description.
listII: i. items that move together are grouped
ii. items near each other are grouped
iii. items that look alike are grouped
iv. incomplete figures are perceived as complete
why: Proximity groups near items (1-ii). Similarity groups alike items (2-iii). Closure completes incomplete figures (3-iv). Common fate groups items moving together (4-i).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-ii, 2-iii, 3-iv, 4-i matches each principle to its description.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: proximity is not similarity; similarity is not proximity.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: proximity is not similarity; closure is not continuity.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: misassigns all four principles.

stem: Match each physiological-perception concept to its description.
listII: i. three cone types sensitive to different wavelengths
ii. opposing colour pairs such as red-green
iii. cortical cells respond to oriented edges
iv. neurons respond to specific stimulus features
why: Hubel and Wiesel found cortical cells respond to oriented edges (1-iii). Trichromatic theory posits three cone types (2-i). Opponent-process theory uses opposing colour pairs (3-ii). Feature detection is neurons responding to specific stimulus features (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-iii, 2-i, 3-ii, 4-iv matches each concept to its description.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: Hubel and Wiesel are not trichromatic theory.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Hubel and Wiesel are oriented edges (iii), not feature detection generally (iv).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: misassigns all four concepts.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: The physiological approach explains perception in terms of neural mechanisms and sensory receptors.
reason: Hubel and Wiesel demonstrated that cortical cells respond to specific features such as oriented edges.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: the physiological approach locates perception in neural mechanisms. The reason is true and correctly explains it: Hubel and Wiesel's feature-detector cells exemplify how neural mechanisms implement perception.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and the feature-detector finding explains the physiological approach.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

stem: Weber's law states that the just noticeable difference:

options.text: is a constant proportion of the reference stimulus

why: Weber's law states that the just noticeable difference (JND) is a constant proportion of the stimulus intensity (Delta I / I = constant). It is not a fixed absolute amount nor the absolute threshold.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: Weber's law is a constant proportion, not a constant absolute amount.
optWhy.B: Correct: Delta I / I is constant; the JND scales with stimulus intensity.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the absolute threshold is the minimum detectable intensity, distinct from the JND.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Weber's law is linear proportionality, not exponential increase.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: According to Weber's law, the just noticeable difference between two stimuli is a constant proportion of the reference stimulus.
reason: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: Weber's law states Delta I / I is constant. The reason is true: the absolute threshold is the intensity detected 50% of the time. However, the reason merely defines absolute threshold; it does not explain why the JND is a constant proportion.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: the reason defines absolute threshold but does not explain Weber's law.
optWhy.B: Correct: both true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

sub: Feature Integration Theory and Automatic/Controlled Processing
stem: Consider the following statements.
statements: 1. Feature Integration Theory assigns focused attention a role in binding features into objects.
2. Automatic processing consumes substantial attentional capacity.
3. Controlled processing is slow, voluntary and capacity-demanding.
4. Illusory conjunctions reflect a failure of feature binding under inattention.
why: Statement 1 is correct: focused attention binds features in FIT. Statement 2 is false: automatic processing consumes little or no capacity. Statement 3 is correct: controlled processing is slow, voluntary and capacity-demanding. Statement 4 is correct: illusory conjunctions are binding failures under inattention. Therefore 1, 3 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 3 and 4 are true; statement 2 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Automatic processes can interfere with performance on controlled tasks.
reason: The Stroop effect shows that involuntary word reading interferes with voluntary colour naming.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: automatic processes can intrude on controlled tasks. The reason is true and correctly explains it: the Stroop effect demonstrates involuntary word reading interfering with voluntary colour naming.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and the Stroop effect explains automatic interference with controlled processing.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

sub: Approaches to Perception: Gestalt and Physiological
stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Gestalt and physiological approaches to perception are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.
reason: Gestalt principles describe organisational regularities while physiological research identifies the neural mechanisms that implement perception.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: Gestalt (organisation/laws) and physiology (neural mechanisms) address different levels of analysis and complement each other. The reason is true and correctly explains it: they describe organisational regularities and neural implementation respectively.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and the levels-of-analysis point explains the complementarity.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

stem: Bottom-up processing in perception is best described as:

options.text: data-driven, from sensory input to perception

why: Bottom-up processing is data-driven: perception begins with sensory input and builds up to a perceptual interpretation. Top-down processing is the conceptually driven direction, guided by expectations and knowledge.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: driven by concepts and expectations describes top-down processing.
optWhy.B: Correct: bottom-up processing is data-driven, from sensory input to perception.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: conscious effort is not a defining feature of bottom-up processing.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: bottom-up processing is driven by the stimulus, not independent of it.

stem: A person expects to see a postman and mistakes a stranger for the postman. This illustrates:
why: The person's prior expectation (postman) shapes the perception of an ambiguous stimulus (the stranger). This is top-down processing: knowledge and expectations influence how sensory input is interpreted.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: pure bottom-up processing would be driven by the sensory data alone, not by expectation.
optWhy.B: Correct: expectation guides interpretation, the hallmark of top-down processing.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: sensory adaptation is reduced responsiveness to unchanging stimulation.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: perceptual constancy is perceiving an object as stable despite changing input.

stem: Consider the following statements about the information-processing approach to perception.
statements: 1. It models perception as stages of encoding, transformation and output.
2. It uses the computer metaphor for cognition.
3. It claims perception is entirely bottom-up with no top-down influence.
4. It is compatible with both bottom-up and top-down processing.
why: Statement 1 is correct: perception is modelled as stages of encoding, transformation and output. Statement 2 is correct: the computer metaphor is central. Statement 3 is false: information-processing accounts allow both bottom-up and top-down influence. Statement 4 is correct. Therefore 1, 2 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: A viewer identifies a printed word by first recognising individual letters and then combining them into the word. This is characteristic of:
why: Recognising letters first and combining them into a word proceeds from the sensory data upward, which is bottom-up, data-driven processing. Top-down processing would use context or expectation to identify the word directly.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: purely top-down processing would not begin with individual letters.
optWhy.B: Correct: letter recognition then word assembly is bottom-up, data-driven processing.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: sensory adaptation is unrelated to letter-by-letter word recognition.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: perceptual constancy concerns stability of perceived object properties.

sub: Gestalt Principles: Continuity, Pragnanz, Good Continuation
stem: The Gestalt principle of Pragnanz (good figure) holds that people organise stimuli into:

options.text: the simplest, most stable and regular form possible

why: Pragnanz states that perception organises stimuli into the simplest, most stable and regular (good) form possible, given the conditions. It is not about complexity, randomness, or familiarity alone.

optWhy.A: Correct: Pragnanz favours the simplest, most stable, regular organisation.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: Pragnanz favours simplicity, not complexity.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: random groupings are not preferred under Pragnanz.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: familiarity is not the criterion of Pragnanz.

key: Gestalt principle of Pragnanz / good figure

sub: Gestalt Principles: Continuity, Pragnanz, Good Continuation
stem: A viewer sees a dotted line as a single continuous line rather than separate dots. This reflects:
why: Good continuation leads the visual system to perceive smooth, continuous lines rather than abrupt changes or separate elements. A dotted line aligned along a path is seen as a continuous line.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: closure concerns completing incomplete figures.
optWhy.B: Correct: good continuation perceives aligned elements as a continuous line.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: common fate concerns items moving together.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: proximity concerns items near each other.

sub: Gestalt Principles: Common Fate, Symmetry, Grouping
stem: Match each Gestalt principle to its description.
listII: i. items moving together are perceived as one group
ii. symmetrical elements are perceived as a unified whole
iii. the tendency to perceive elements as grouped
why: Common fate groups items that move together (1-i). Symmetry perceives symmetrical elements as a unified whole (2-ii). Grouping is the general tendency to perceive elements as grouped (3-iii).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-i, 2-ii, 3-iii matches each principle to its description.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: common fate is movement (i), not symmetry (ii).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: common fate is movement (i), not grouping (iii).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: misassigns all three principles.

key: Gestalt principles of common fate, symmetry and grouping

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: In Rubin's vase figure, the same stimulus can be perceived as either a vase or two faces.
reason: Figure and ground can reverse, with either region serving as the focal figure.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: Rubin's vase is a reversible figure-ground stimulus. The reason is true and correctly explains it: the same contour can bound either the vase (as figure) or the faces (as figure), with the other region becoming ground.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and figure-ground reversal explains the vase/faces perception.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

stem: In figure-ground perception, the figure is:

options.text: the focal object against the ground

why: The figure is the focal object or region that stands out against the ground (background). The figure is not defined by being smaller or larger; it is defined by being the focus of attention.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: the figure is not always the smaller region.
optWhy.B: Correct: the figure is the focal object perceived against the ground.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the background region is the ground, not the figure.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the figure is not defined by being the larger region.

stem: Consider the following statements about Gestalt organisational principles.
statements: 1. Gestalt principles describe how stimuli tend to be organised.
2. Gestalt principles always predict perception unambiguously.
3. Ambiguous figures show that organisation can reverse.
4. Context and experience can influence which grouping prevails.
why: Statement 1 is correct: Gestalt principles describe organisational tendencies. Statement 2 is false: principles do not always predict perception unambiguously (ambiguous figures reverse). Statement 3 is correct: ambiguous figures show reversible organisation. Statement 4 is correct: context and experience influence grouping. Therefore 1, 3 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 3 and 4 are true; statement 2 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.

sub: Perceptual Constancy: Size, Shape, Colour, Brightness
stem: Size constancy refers to the perception that:

options.text: an object's physical size changes with distance
an object is perceived as the same size despite changes in retinal image size
all objects appear the same size
size is judged only by retinal image size

why: Size constancy is the perception of an object as having a stable size even though its retinal image changes with distance. The perceptual system uses distance cues to compensate for retinal-image changes.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: physical size does not change with distance; perception compensates for retinal change.
optWhy.B: Correct: the object is perceived as the same size despite retinal-image changes.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: objects do not all appear the same size; constancy applies to a given object.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: size constancy means perception is not based only on retinal image size.

sub: Perceptual Constancy: Size, Shape, Colour, Brightness
stem: A car appears to be the same size whether it is nearby or far away, even though its retinal image shrinks with distance. This is:
why: The car is perceived as stable in size despite a changing retinal image. This is size constancy: distance cues compensate for the smaller retinal image of the distant car.

optWhy.A: Correct: stable perceived size despite changing retinal image is size constancy.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the Muller-Lyer illusion is a line-length illusion, not size constancy.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: sensory adaptation is reduced responsiveness to unchanging stimulation.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: change blindness is failure to notice changes between views.

stem: Consider the following statements about factors influencing perceptual constancy.
statements: 2. Familiarity with an object supports constancy.
3. Constancy is perfect under all viewing conditions.
4. Atmospheric perspective can support distance perception.
why: Statement 1 is correct: distance cues support size constancy. Statement 2 is correct: familiarity with an object's typical size supports constancy. Statement 3 is false: constancy is not perfect under all conditions (for example, extreme distances or impoverished cues). Statement 4 is correct: atmospheric perspective (haze, contrast) supports distance perception. Therefore 1, 2 and 4 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: The moon appears larger near the horizon than overhead, partly because horizon distance cues (terrain, buildings) support greater perceived distance. This relates to:

options.text: size constancy and the moon illusion

why: The moon illusion is explained in part by size constancy: horizon distance cues make the moon seem farther away, so the same-sized retinal image is perceived as a larger object. Sensory adaptation, change blindness and echoic persistence are unrelated.

optWhy.A: Correct: distance cues and size constancy explain the moon illusion.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: sensory adaptation is unrelated to the moon illusion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: change blindness concerns failure to notice changes between views.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: echoic persistence is brief auditory sensory storage.

stem: In the Muller-Lyer illusion, two equal-length lines appear different because arrowheads at the ends alter perceived depth. This is best explained by:
why: Gregory's explanation: the arrowheads act like depth cues (outward arrows resemble the near corners of a room; inward arrows resemble far corners). The line with outward arrowheads is perceived as farther away and therefore larger, despite equal retinal length — a misapplication of size constancy.

optWhy.A: Correct: Gregory's depth-cue/size-constancy explanation of the Muller-Lyer illusion.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: sensory adaptation is unrelated to line-length illusions.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: change blindness concerns failure to notice changes between views.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: echoic persistence is brief auditory sensory storage.

key: Muller-Lyer illusion and misapplied size constancy

stem: Match each perceptual illusion to its explanation.
listII: i. parallel lines converge like railway tracks, altering depth perception
ii. arrowheads alter perceived length via depth cues
iii. moon near horizon appears larger due to distance cues
why: The Muller-Lyer illusion uses arrowheads as depth cues to alter perceived length (1-ii). The Ponzo illusion uses converging parallel lines (like railway tracks) to alter depth (2-i). The moon illusion uses horizon distance cues to make the horizon moon seem larger (3-iii).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-ii, 2-i, 3-iii matches each illusion to its explanation.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: Muller-Lyer is arrowheads (ii), not converging lines (i).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Muller-Lyer is not the moon illusion (iii).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Ponzo is converging lines (i), not horizon cues (iii).

sub: Perception of Depth: Monocular and Binocular Cues
stem: Match each depth cue to its description.
listII: i. binocular cue from the difference between the two eyes' images
ii. binocular cue from the inward turning of the eyes
iii. monocular cue: a nearer object blocks the view of a farther object
iv. monocular cue: parallel lines appear to converge in the distance
why: Retinal disparity is the binocular difference between the two eyes' images (1-i). Convergence is the inward turning of the eyes for near objects (2-ii). Occlusion is a monocular cue where a nearer object blocks a farther one (3-iii). Linear perspective is the convergence of parallel lines in distance (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-i, 2-ii, 3-iii, 4-iv matches each depth cue to its description.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: retinal disparity is binocular image difference (i), not convergence (ii).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: occlusion is blocking (iii), not retinal disparity (i).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: misassigns all four cues.

stem: Recognition-by-components (RBC) theory proposes that objects are recognised by:

options.text: matching the whole image to a stored template
decomposing objects into geometric components (geons) and their relations
matching to a single ideal prototype

why: Biederman's recognition-by-components theory proposes that objects are decomposed into simple geometric components (geons, such as cubes and cylinders) and their relations, which are then matched to stored structural descriptions. It is not whole-image template matching, exemplar averaging, or single-prototype matching.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: whole-image matching is template matching, not RBC.
optWhy.B: Correct: RBC decomposes objects into geons and their relations.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: averaging exemplars is an exemplar/prototype approach, not RBC.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: matching to a single ideal prototype is prototype theory, not RBC.

stem: Match each form-perception theory to its description.
listII: i. match the stimulus to a stored average or best example
ii. detect component features of the stimulus
iii. compare the stimulus to stored whole-shape templates
iv. decompose objects into geometric components and their relations
why: Template matching compares the stimulus to stored whole-shape templates (1-iii). Prototype matching matches to a stored average or best example (2-i). Feature analysis detects component features (3-ii). Recognition-by-components decomposes objects into geons and relations (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-iii, 2-i, 3-ii, 4-iv matches each theory to its description.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: template matching is whole-shape templates (iii), not average (i).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: template matching is not feature detection (ii).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: prototype matching is average/best example (i), not features (ii).

sub: Perception of Depth: Monocular and Binocular Cues
stem: A painter depicts railway tracks that appear to converge in the distance to create a sense of depth on a flat canvas. The depth cue used is:
why: Linear perspective is a monocular depth cue in which parallel lines appear to converge as they recede into the distance. Retinal disparity and convergence are binocular cues requiring two eyes; accommodation is a cue to distance based on lens focusing.

optWhy.A: Correct: converging parallel lines on a flat surface is linear perspective.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: retinal disparity requires two eyes and is not a cue available from a flat canvas.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: convergence is a binocular cue based on eye turning.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: accommodation concerns lens focusing for near/far objects.

sub: Perception of Depth: Monocular and Binocular Cues
stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Binocular depth cues require the use of both eyes.
reason: Retinal disparity and convergence are binocular cues.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: binocular cues require both eyes. The reason is true and correctly explains it: retinal disparity (difference between the two retinal images) and convergence (inward eye turning) are binocular cues.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and retinal disparity/convergence explain why binocular cues need both eyes.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

key: Binocular depth cues require both eyes

stem: In Sherif's autokinetic-effect experiment, a stationary point of light in a dark room appears to move, and when participants judge the movement in groups, their estimates converge over time. This demonstrates:

options.text: apparent movement and the formation of a group norm

why: The autokinetic effect is apparent movement of a stationary light in a dark frame (due to small eye movements and lack of reference points). Sherif used it to show norm formation: group members' estimates converge on a shared standard.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: the light is stationary; the movement is apparent, not real.
optWhy.B: Correct: apparent movement and group norm formation.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: sensory adaptation is reduced responsiveness to unchanging stimulation.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: change blindness is failure to notice changes between views.

key: Autokinetic effect and group norm formation

stem: Consider the following statements about movement perception.
statements: 1. Apparent movement (phi phenomenon) is perceived motion between static stimuli presented in succession.
2. Stroboscopic movement makes continuous motion appear as discrete steps.
3. Induced movement makes a stationary object appear to move because a surrounding object moves.
4. The autokinetic effect is real movement of a stationary light.
why: Statement 1 is correct: phi/apparent movement is perceived motion between successive static stimuli. Statement 2 is correct: stroboscopic movement samples continuous motion, making it appear discrete. Statement 3 is correct: induced movement makes a stationary object seem to move when a surrounding frame moves. Statement 4 is false: the autokinetic effect is apparent, not real, movement. Therefore 1, 2 and 3 only.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 3 are true; statement 4 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is also true.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 4 is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 4 is false.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Bottom-up and top-down processing both contribute to perception.
reason: Sensory data drives recognition while expectations and context shape interpretation.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: perception involves both bottom-up (data-driven) and top-down (conceptually driven) processing. The reason is true and correctly explains it: sensory data drives recognition from the input upward, while expectations and context shape interpretation from the top down.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and the complementary roles explain the joint contribution.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Perceptual constancy and perceptual illusions can both arise from the operation of constancy mechanisms.
reason: The Muller-Lyer illusion is explained by misapplied size constancy, while size constancy itself stabilises perception across distance.

options.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
Assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, but reason is true.

why: The assertion is true: constancy mechanisms normally stabilise perception, but when misapplied (for example, depth cues in the Muller-Lyer illusion) they produce illusions. The reason is true and correctly explains it: size constancy stabilises size perception, and its misapplication explains the Muller-Lyer illusion.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true, and the misapplied-constancy explanation accounts for both constancy and illusion.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the reason is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the assertion is true.

key: Constancy mechanisms produce both constancy and illusion

sub: Signal Detection Theory: assumptions and signal versus noise
stem: In signal detection theory, the observer's decision about whether a signal is present depends on:

options.text: the sensory evidence combined with a decision criterion
the physical intensity of the signal only

why: Signal detection theory models each decision as a function of the sensory evidence (signal plus noise) and the observer's decision criterion (how much evidence is required to say "signal present"). This separates sensitivity from response bias.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: the absolute threshold is only one classical concept; SDT adds the criterion and noise.
optWhy.B: Correct: the decision rests on sensory evidence and the decision criterion.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: signal intensity alone does not determine the decision; noise and criterion matter too.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: motivation may influence the criterion but is not the sole determinant.

key: SDT decision: sensory evidence plus decision criterion

sub: Signal Detection Theory: assumptions and signal versus noise
stem: A radiologist examining an X-ray must decide whether a faint shadow indicates a tumour. In signal detection terms, the faint shadow is the:
why: The faint shadow is the potential signal the observer is trying to detect. The decision (tumour present or absent) is made by comparing the sensory evidence to a criterion. Noise is the background variability; the criterion is the threshold for saying "present"; a hit is a correct detection.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: noise is the background variability, not the shadow being judged.
optWhy.B: Correct: the faint shadow is the potential signal.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the criterion is the decision rule, not the stimulus.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: a hit is a correct detection outcome, not the stimulus itself.

sub: Signal Detection Theory: sensitivity and decision criterion
stem: Consider the following statements about signal detection theory.
statements: 1. Sensitivity (d prime) reflects how well the observer can discriminate signal from noise.
2. The decision criterion (beta) reflects the observer's willingness to say "signal present."
3. A liberal criterion increases both hits and false alarms.
4. Sensitivity and criterion are independent; one can change without the other.
why: All four statements are correct. d′ measures sensitivity (discriminability); beta measures the criterion/bias; a liberal criterion (low threshold for "present") raises both hits and false alarms; and sensitivity and criterion are independent dimensions in SDT.

optWhy.A: Correct: all four statements are true.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statements 3 and 4 are also true.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statements 1 and 3 are also true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 2 is also true.

sub: Signal Detection Theory: sensitivity and decision criterion
stem: A participant has a hit rate of 0.84 and a false-alarm rate of 0.16. These correspond to z-scores of approximately +1.0 and -1.0, so d prime equals:
why: d prime = z(hit rate) − z(false-alarm rate) = 1.0 − (−1.0) = 2. A d prime of 2 indicates good discriminability between signal and noise.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: d prime is not zero; the hit rate exceeds the false-alarm rate.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: d prime is 1.0 minus (-1.0), which is 2, not 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: d prime is a difference of z-scores, not their product or sum.

key: Calculating d prime from hit and false-alarm rates

sub: Signal Detection Theory: sensitivity and decision criterion
stem: If an observer shifts to a more liberal decision criterion while sensitivity stays the same, then:

options.text: d prime is unchanged, but both hits and false alarms rise
hits fall and false alarms rise

why: Sensitivity (d prime) is independent of the criterion. A more liberal criterion lowers the threshold for saying "signal present," so both hits and false alarms increase while d prime remains constant.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: d prime is independent of the criterion and does not increase.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: d prime does not decrease with a criterion shift.
optWhy.C: Correct: d prime is unchanged; a liberal criterion raises both hits and false alarms.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: hits rise, not fall, under a liberal criterion.

key: Criterion shift does not change d prime

sub: Signal Detection Theory: hit, miss, false alarm, correct rejection
stem: In signal detection theory, a "false alarm" occurs when:

options.text: the signal is present and the observer says "present"
the signal is absent and the observer says "present"
the signal is present and the observer says "absent"
the signal is absent and the observer says "absent"

why: A false alarm is a false positive: saying "signal present" when no signal was actually present. A hit is present-and-say-present; a miss is present-and-say-absent; a correct rejection is absent-and-say-absent.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: present and say present is a hit, not a false alarm.
optWhy.B: Correct: absent but say present is a false alarm.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: present and say absent is a miss.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: absent and say absent is a correct rejection.

sub: Signal Detection Theory: hit, miss, false alarm, correct rejection
stem: A smoke alarm sounds when there is no fire. In signal detection terms, this is a:
why: There is no signal (no fire) but the system says "present" (alarm sounds). That is a false alarm (false positive).

optWhy.A: Incorrect: a hit requires a real signal correctly detected.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: a miss is failing to detect a real signal.
optWhy.C: Correct: no signal but a positive response is a false alarm.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: a correct rejection is correctly saying "absent" when no signal is present.

sub: Signal Detection Theory: ROC curves and applications
stem: Consider the following statements about ROC curves in signal detection theory.
statements: 1. An ROC curve plots hit rate against false-alarm rate across criteria.
2. The area under the ROC curve reflects sensitivity.
3. Changing the criterion moves the observer along the ROC curve.
4. Changing sensitivity moves the ROC curve itself.
why: All four statements are correct. An ROC curve plots hit rate against false-alarm rate as the criterion varies; the area under the curve reflects sensitivity (d prime); changing the criterion moves the operating point along the curve; and changing sensitivity shifts the curve itself.

optWhy.A: Correct: all four statements are true.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statements 2 and 4 are also true.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statements 1 and 3 are also true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 2 is also true.

sub: Signal Detection Theory: ROC curves and applications
stem: Match each signal detection concept to its description.
listII: i. many hits but also many false alarms
ii. few hits and few false alarms
iii. excellent discrimination between signal and noise
iv. poor discrimination between signal and noise
why: A liberal criterion (low threshold for "present") yields many hits but also many false alarms (1-i). A conservative criterion yields few hits and few false alarms (2-ii). High sensitivity means excellent signal-noise discrimination (3-iii); low sensitivity means poor discrimination (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-i, 2-ii, 3-iii, 4-iv matches each concept to its description.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: a liberal criterion is not few hits and few false alarms.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: misassigns criterion and sensitivity descriptions.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: misassigns all four concepts.

sub: Signal Detection Theory: ROC curves and applications
stem: After training, an observer's ROC curve shifts upward and to the left, giving a higher hit rate for the same false-alarm rate. This indicates that:

options.text: false alarms decreased at all hit rates

why: An upward/leftward shift of the ROC curve (higher hit rate for the same false-alarm rate) indicates improved sensitivity (higher d prime). Criterion changes move the operating point along a curve, not shift the curve itself.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: criterion changes move along the curve, not shift it.
optWhy.B: Correct: an upward/leftward ROC shift indicates improved sensitivity.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: criterion changes move along the curve, not shift it.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the shift means more hits at the same false-alarm rate, not fewer false alarms at all hit rates.

stem: Match each subliminal-perception concept to its description.
listII: ii. minimum intensity detected 50 percent of the time
iii. prior exposure influencing a later response without awareness
why: Subliminal perception is perception below conscious awareness (1-i). The absolute threshold is the minimum intensity detected 50 percent of the time (2-ii). Priming is prior exposure influencing a later response, often without awareness (3-iii). Supraliminal means above conscious awareness (4-iv).

optWhy.A: Correct: 1-i, 2-ii, 3-iii, 4-iv matches each concept to its description.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: subliminal perception is below awareness (i), not the threshold (ii).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: misassigns subliminal perception and priming.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: misassigns all four concepts.

stem: A researcher presents a word so briefly that participants cannot report seeing it, yet their later judgements are biased by the word. This is:
why: Presentation below the threshold of conscious awareness that still influences later judgements is subliminal perception (subliminal priming). Effects are generally modest and short-lived.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: supraliminal perception is above conscious awareness.
optWhy.B: Correct: below-awareness presentation influencing later judgements is subliminal perception.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: sensory adaptation is reduced responsiveness to unchanging stimulation.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: change blindness is failure to notice changes between views.

stem: Assess the assertion and reason.
assertion: Subliminal perception can influence behaviour without conscious awareness.
