why: Corresponding points are associated with the horopter; small disparities can fuse and support stereopsis; greater disparities can yield double vision when neither image is suppressed; convergence concerns eye orientation, not retinal disparity itself.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Retinal locations with the same visual direction at a specified fixation), not a; 2 should match c (A disparity that may support a single percept with stereoscopic depth), not b; 3 should match d (A mismatch that can result in diplopia when both images are visible), not c; 4 should match a (Eye rotation that aligns the visual axes on a target), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 2 should match c (A disparity that may support a single percept with stereoscopic depth), not a; 4 should match a (Eye rotation that aligns the visual axes on a target), not c.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Retinal locations with the same visual direction at a specified fixation), not d; 3 should match d (A mismatch that can result in diplopia when both images are visible), not b.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–b (Corresponding retinal points: Retinal locations with the same visual direction at a specified fixation); 2–c (Small nonzero fusible disparity: A disparity that may support a single percept with stereoscopic depth); 3–d (Disparity beyond the applicable fusional range: A mismatch that can result in diplopia when both images are visible); 4–a (Convergence: Eye rotation that aligns the visual axes on a target).

key: Retinal correspondence, fusion and eye orientation

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: Template approaches compare input to stored patterns; feature analysis extracts elements; recognition by components represents geons and relations; top-down context uses knowledge or expectations. These approaches are not necessarily mutually exclusive in a complete system.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Comparison of input with stored pattern representations), not a; 2 should match a (Extraction of diagnostic local elements such as edges or line orientations), not b; 3 should match d (Recovery of volumetric components and their structural relations), not c; 4 should match c (Use of expectations or context to bias recognition of ambiguous input), not d.
optWhy.B: Correct: 1–b (Template matching: Comparison of input with stored pattern representations); 2–a (Feature analysis: Extraction of diagnostic local elements such as edges or line orientations); 3–d (Recognition by components: Recovery of volumetric components and their structural relations); 4–c (Top-down contextual influence: Use of expectations or context to bias recognition of ambiguous input).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Comparison of input with stored pattern representations), not c; 2 should match a (Extraction of diagnostic local elements such as edges or line orientations), not d; 3 should match d (Recovery of volumetric components and their structural relations), not b; 4 should match c (Use of expectations or context to bias recognition of ambiguous input), not a.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Comparison of input with stored pattern representations), not d; 2 should match a (Extraction of diagnostic local elements such as edges or line orientations), not c; 3 should match d (Recovery of volumetric components and their structural relations), not a; 4 should match c (Use of expectations or context to bias recognition of ambiguous input), not b.

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: A hit and a miss occur on signal-present trials; a false alarm and a correct rejection occur on signal-absent trials. These are outcome categories, not by themselves measures of sensitivity or criterion.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Abnormality present; observer reports abnormality), not a; 2 should match d (Abnormality present; observer reports no abnormality), not b; 4 should match a (No abnormality present; observer reports no abnormality), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 2 should match d (Abnormality present; observer reports no abnormality), not a; 3 should match c (No abnormality present; observer reports abnormality), not d; 4 should match a (No abnormality present; observer reports no abnormality), not c.
optWhy.C: Correct: 1–b (Hit: Abnormality present; observer reports abnormality); 2–d (Miss: Abnormality present; observer reports no abnormality); 3–c (False alarm: No abnormality present; observer reports abnormality); 4–a (Correct rejection: No abnormality present; observer reports no abnormality).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Abnormality present; observer reports abnormality), not c; 3 should match c (No abnormality present; observer reports abnormality), not a; 4 should match a (No abnormality present; observer reports no abnormality), not b.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: occlusion gives relative ordering, not exact separation. 2 is true: learned typical size can inform distance. 3 is false: perspective is available in a monocular picture. 4 is true: accommodation changes lens focus in an eye, especially informing near distance.

optWhy.A: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2, 4.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true by the corresponding-point definition. 2 is false because small disparities may lie within the fusional range. 3 is true in suitable binocular conditions. 4 is true: eye orientation and retinal disparity are distinct physiological quantities.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 2 and omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 2 and omits true statement(s) 1, 3.
optWhy.C: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 3, 4.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 2.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: local features can contribute to recognition. 2 is true of a rigid single-template implementation, not every template-based system. 3 is true: geons and their relations are central to Biederman’s account. 4 is false: context and sensory evidence can interact.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.D: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 3.

key: Comparing feature, template and structural accounts

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: perceived shape can remain comparatively stable across projection changes. 2 is true as a distinction between apparent surface lightness and physical luminance. 3 is false: brightness and lightness are perceptual attributes, not physical units. 4 is true as a qualified tendency; constancy is not always perfect.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: false alarms are divided by signal-absent trials. 2 is true under the stated model and z convention. 3 is false: a single point cannot test equal variance. 4 is true: criteria generate operating points from fixed distributions.

optWhy.A: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2, 4.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true by definition. 2 is true: misses are signal-present; correct rejections are signal-absent. 3 is true: payoff incentives can affect criterion. 4 is false: the false-alarm rate uses the number of signal-absent trials as its denominator.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.D: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 3.

stem: A pilot views two otherwise comparable runways from the same actual distance. One is physically narrower, so its width subtends a smaller visual angle. If the pilot mistakenly assumes both runways have the same standard width, which distance inference is plausible?

options.text: The narrower runway must be closer because accommodation is identical.
The narrower runway may be judged farther away on the basis of assumed familiar width.
The narrower runway must have greater binocular disparity in a flat photograph.
The angular width alone proves the true distance without any size assumption.

why: With the same assumed physical width, a smaller angular width is consistent with a greater inferred distance. The narrower runway violates the size assumption, so this inference can be misleading. The scenario does not establish any particular aircraft manoeuvre.

optWhy.A: A reverses the size–distance inference and invokes accommodation without supporting information.
optWhy.B: B correctly applies an assumed familiar width to the smaller angular projection.
optWhy.C: C introduces an unspecified photograph and asserts a disparity difference not established by runway width.
optWhy.D: D ignores the ambiguity between actual size and distance.

key: Familiar size and misleading distance inference

stem: In a drawing, disk A overlaps disk B, but A is drawn smaller than B. An observer reports A as nearer because its contour interrupts B. Which interpretation is most defensible?

options.text: The smaller projected size proves A is physically smaller.
Retinal disparity must have determined the report.
Relative size can never influence the depth of drawn objects.
Interposition favours A as nearer even though size information could favour another ordering under an equal-size assumption.

why: A’s occluding contour gives an ordinal interposition cue that places A in front. If disks are assumed equal in physical size, their relative projected sizes can favour the opposite distance ordering. The result illustrates cue competition, not a universal hierarchy.

optWhy.A: A ignores the size–distance ambiguity and does not follow from the drawing alone.
optWhy.B: B assumes binocular disparity even though a drawing can supply monocular cues.
optWhy.C: C wrongly excludes relative size as a pictorial cue.
optWhy.D: D correctly identifies the conflicting conditional inferences.

stem: During steady binocular fixation, a clinician presents a small target with nonzero disparity known to be within the patient’s measured fusional range. Both eyes contribute and the target is reported as single and displaced in depth. What interpretation best fits?

options.text: The target must lie exactly on corresponding retinal points.
The single percept proves that stereoscopic depth is impossible.
Fusion of a small disparity is compatible with stereopsis away from exact correspondence.
Convergence and disparity are necessarily identical numerical quantities.

why: A small nonzero disparity can be fused and convey relative stereoscopic depth, provided both eyes contribute. Single vision does not imply zero disparity or that the point lies on the horopter. The measured range and binocular contribution rule out some alternative explanations.

optWhy.A: A wrongly equates single vision with exact correspondence.
optWhy.B: B ignores stereopsis from small fused disparities.
optWhy.C: C correctly interprets fusion of nonzero disparity.
optWhy.D: D conflates eye-orientation geometry with retinal image disparity.

stem: A radiologist assesses 10,000 abnormal and 10,000 normal images, with 8,413 hits and 1,587 false alarms respectively. Assume equal-variance Gaussian evidence and use z(p) as the inverse standard-normal cumulative function, with z(0.8413)=1.00 and z(0.1587)=-1.00. Using d′=z(H)-z(F), what is d′?
why: The theoretical hit rate H is 0.8413 and false-alarm rate F is 0.1587. With the supplied z values, d′=1.00−(−1.00)=2.00. The rates use the appropriate signal-present and signal-absent denominators; neither is a boundary rate.

optWhy.A: A would result from incorrectly adding opposite z-scores.
optWhy.B: B is correct: subtracting −1.00 from 1.00 gives 2.00.
optWhy.C: C is half the standardised separation under the stated formula.
optWhy.D: D reverses the order of subtraction.

stem: Two yes/no conditions have H and F rates A=(0.8413, 0.1587) and B=(0.9772, 0.5000). Assume equal-variance Gaussian evidence; z is the inverse standard-normal cumulative function; use z(0.8413)=1, z(0.1587)=-1, z(0.9772)=2 and z(0.5000)=0. Let d′=z(H)-z(F) and c=-[z(H)+z(F)]/2; a smaller c indicates a more liberal criterion. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Both have d′=2; B has a more liberal criterion than A.
Both have d′=2; B has a more conservative criterion than A.
B has higher d′ and the same criterion as A.
A has higher d′ and a more liberal criterion than B.

why: Condition A has d′=1−(−1)=2 and c=−(1−1)/2=0. Condition B has d′=2−0=2 and c=−(2+0)/2=−1. With the stated convention, the more negative criterion is more liberal. Rounded z values are treated as exact for this exercise.

optWhy.A: A is correct: sensitivity estimates are equal and B’s criterion is more liberal.
optWhy.B: B reverses the direction indicated by the negative c value.
optWhy.C: C overlooks that both d′ estimates equal 2 and the c estimates differ.
optWhy.D: D reverses the equal sensitivity result and the criterion ordering.

stem: A laboratory increases the penalty for false alarms. Before the change H=0.8413 and F=0.5000; afterwards H=0.5000 and F=0.1587. Assume fixed equal-variance Gaussian evidence distributions and a yes response above criterion. Let z be the inverse standard-normal cumulative function, with z(0.8413)=1, z(0.5000)=0 and z(0.1587)=-1. Use d′=z(H)-z(F), c=-[z(H)+z(F)]/2 and β=exp(d′c), the signal-plus-noise to noise likelihood ratio at the criterion. What are the after-change values?
why: After the change, d′=0−(−1)=1 and c=−(0−1)/2=0.5. Thus β=exp(1×0.5)≈1.65. Before the change, d′=1 and c=−0.5, consistent with a more conservative criterion after the penalty and unchanged modelled sensitivity.

optWhy.A: A uses the wrong separation and criterion.
optWhy.B: B gives the pre-change criterion and β, not the after-change values.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly sets the separation to zero and inconsistently evaluates β.
optWhy.D: D correctly calculates d′, c and β and identifies a conservative shift.

sub: Degraded object recognition and structural description
stem: A researcher masks equal amounts of contour in two versions of object drawings. One mask preserves part junctions and the other removes junctions needed to identify component relations. Recognition is better in the junction-preserved condition. What interpretation best fits?

options.text: The result proves every object is recognised by one stored retinal template.
The result proves context can never influence recognition.
The result is consistent with component-and-relation recovery, although other differences between masks must be assessed.
The result demonstrates that contour information is irrelevant.

why: Recognition-by-components predicts that preserving diagnostic component structure can help recognition even when images are degraded. The result is consistent with that prediction but does not uniquely prove the theory; visibility, salience and other masking differences should be checked.

optWhy.A: A asserts an exclusive rigid-template mechanism that does not follow from the contrast.
optWhy.B: B makes an unrelated universal claim about context.
optWhy.C: C correctly connects the result to structural recovery while acknowledging alternative explanations.
optWhy.D: D contradicts the observed effect of changing which contours and junctions remain.

stem: For a yes/no task, suppose Gaussian noise and signal-plus-noise evidence have standard deviations σN and σS. Let z be the inverse standard-normal cumulative function. In a z-ROC, plot z(H) vertically against z(F) horizontally; its slope equals σN/σS. Two fitted points are (z(F), z(H))=(-1.0, 0.5) and (0.0, 1.0). What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The slope is 0.5, so σS is twice σN; the equal-variance assumption is not supported by this fitted slope.
The slope is 2.0, so σN is twice σS.
The slope is 1.0, establishing equal variances.
The slope is 0.5, proving that both conditions have zero sensitivity.

why: The slope is (1.0−0.5)/(0.0−(−1.0))=0.5. Given slope=σN/σS, σS=2σN. A fitted slope different from 1 is inconsistent with the equal-variance Gaussian model, subject to uncertainty in real data. It does not by itself imply zero discriminability.

optWhy.A: A correctly calculates the slope and applies the stated variance ratio.
optWhy.B: B takes the reciprocal of the given slope relation.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly calculates the slope and asserts equal variance.
optWhy.D: D confuses a variance ratio with zero separation of the evidence distributions.

stem: A cat repeatedly escapes a puzzle box by operating a latch. Its escape latency generally decreases across trials, with some fluctuations. Which classical interpretation is most consistent with Thorndike’s law of effect?

options.text: The cat must have mentally solved the box before any movement occurred.
Responses followed by satisfying consequences tend to strengthen their connection with the situation.
The physical position of the latch is learned only through binocular disparity.
Every response performed in the box is strengthened equally, regardless of its consequences.

why: Thorndike interpreted gradual improvement as trial-and-error selection: responses followed by satisfying outcomes become more likely in the situation. Escape latency is a performance measure, and the curve alone does not conclusively rule out all other mechanisms.

optWhy.A: A asserts unobserved insight as a necessary explanation.
optWhy.B: B correctly identifies the consequence-sensitive strengthening of the situation–response connection.
optWhy.C: C introduces a perceptual mechanism unrelated to the stated law.
optWhy.D: D ignores Thorndike’s distinction between effective and ineffective consequences.

key: Law of effect and trial-and-error performance

stem: Which comparison best represents Thorndike’s early and later formulations without treating his historical interpretation as a universal modern finding?

options.text: He originally rejected all effects of consequences and later made punishment the sole source of learning.
He retained an exact symmetry: rewards and punishments necessarily change connection strength equally in opposite directions.
He concluded that satisfying consequences never strengthen responses.
He initially proposed strengthening by satisfaction and weakening by annoyance, but later judged reward and punishment effects to be substantially asymmetric.

why: The original law described satisfying outcomes as strengthening and annoying outcomes as weakening connections. Thorndike later placed greater weight on reward and questioned a comparable direct weakening effect of punishment. This historical revision does not imply that punishment can never suppress behaviour.

optWhy.A: A reverses the historical position on consequences.
optWhy.B: B incorrectly preserves the original symmetry in the revised account.
optWhy.C: C contradicts the continuing role of satisfying consequences.
optWhy.D: D correctly contrasts the early two-sided formulation with the later asymmetry.

key: Revision of the law of effect

stem: Two equally trained animals are tested without additional reinforcement. One is more food-deprived than the other, while the same food reward is signalled to both. Which Hullian distinction best describes the manipulation?

options.text: The deprivation difference primarily changes drive; it need not imply a difference in established habit strength.
The deprivation difference is identical to changing the size of the reward.
The differing response rates prove that the animals formed different numbers of stimulus–response associations during training.
Drive is a synonym for conditioned inhibition and cannot energise performance.

why: In Hull’s system habit strength reflects reinforced learning history, whereas drive energises performance. With training and incentive held comparable, altered deprivation is intended to manipulate drive, though actual deprivation can have additional effects. Performance differences alone do not measure habit directly.

optWhy.A: A correctly separates motivational state from prior habit strength.
optWhy.B: B confuses drive associated with deprivation with incentive associated with the goal.
optWhy.C: C infers a training difference that the scenario does not establish.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly equates an energising variable with an inhibitory process.

stem: A novice slowly masters a complex keyboard sequence over many sessions. Why is that observation not automatically incompatible with Guthrie’s one-trial learning claim?

options.text: Guthrie claimed complex skills require no practice and appear complete at the first attempt.
He proposed that reward must incrementally strengthen every individual connection.
A complex act involves many movement–cue associations and changing stimulus situations, even if a particular association forms in one pairing.
He equated the number of practice sessions with the number of reinforcers required by Hull.

why: Guthrie’s one-trial claim concerns a particular stimulus-pattern and movement association, not complete mastery of an entire skill. Repeated practice can expose many cue combinations and movements, producing gradual improvement in the larger act.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly extends one-trial association to complete mastery.
optWhy.B: B substitutes a reinforcement-based incremental mechanism for Guthrie’s contiguity account.
optWhy.C: C correctly distinguishes discrete associations from a complex act.
optWhy.D: D confuses Guthrie’s account with a reinforcement-count rule.

stem: In a controlled study, a response is paired once with a novel cue without programmed reward. A later test shows that the cue increases the probability of that response. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: The result uniquely proves Guthrie’s complete theory.
The result is compatible with association without programmed reinforcement, but alternative sources of reinforcement and other learning mechanisms need control.
The result proves that reward can never affect learning.
The result establishes that every complex act reaches asymptote after one trial.

why: An effect after one unrewarded programmed pairing is compatible with Guthrie’s contiguity claim. However, unprogrammed consequences, pre-existing biases and other associative mechanisms must be considered; one result does not uniquely establish an entire theory.

optWhy.A: A overclaims that one observation uniquely identifies a theory.
optWhy.B: B correctly describes the evidence and key alternative explanations.
optWhy.C: C wrongly generalises absence of programmed reward into a universal claim about reward.
optWhy.D: D conflates one association with mastery of every complex skill.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Gradual improvement in a complex act does not by itself disprove Guthrie’s one-trial account.
reason: Guthrie distinguished a complex act from the many specific movement–stimulus associations that may be encountered across trials.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: Both statements are true. The reason explains why overall performance can improve gradually even if each particular association is assumed to form in one trial. The resulting learning curve does not by itself decide between Guthrie’s and incremental accounts.

optWhy.A: A is correct: acquiring different specific associations can yield a gradual act-level curve.
optWhy.B: B overlooks the explanatory connection between the distinction and gradual performance.
optWhy.C: C wrongly rejects Guthrie’s movement–act distinction.
optWhy.D: D wrongly treats gradual performance as a decisive refutation of the specified account.

key: Performance curves versus assumed association formation

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Thorndike’s later revision proves that punishment can never reduce an observable response under any conditions.
reason: In his later account, Thorndike questioned whether annoying consequences weaken a connection as directly and symmetrically as satisfying consequences strengthen it.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is false: a historical revision does not establish that punishment can never suppress observable behaviour. The reason is true as a summary of Thorndike’s later asymmetry; suppression and direct weakening of a connection are not identical claims.

optWhy.A: A wrongly treats the universal claim about punishment as established.
optWhy.B: B wrongly accepts the assertion despite its overgeneralisation.
optWhy.C: C reverses the truth values.
optWhy.D: D is correct: Thorndike’s revision concerned asymmetric connection effects, not impossibility of suppression.

key: Historical revision versus observed punishment effects

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A temporary decline in a well-trained animal’s maze speed does not by itself establish that its learned habit has weakened.
reason: Hull aimed to derive testable predictions from explicit theoretical postulates.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true because drive, incentive, inhibition or other performance factors may change without proving a change in habit. The reason is also true about Hull’s hypothetico-deductive method, but it does not explain the specific learning–performance distinction.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly treats the general methodological statement as the explanation of the speed decline.
optWhy.B: B is correct: both statements are true but the reason is not the explanation.
optWhy.C: C wrongly denies Hull’s hypothetico-deductive approach.
optWhy.D: D wrongly assumes reduced performance uniquely proves weaker learning.

key: Habit strength, performance and theory construction

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Guthrie did not regard reinforcement as necessary for formation of every stimulus–movement association.
reason: He treated reward as capable of changing the stimulus situation and thereby protecting the last association from replacement.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: Both statements are true in Guthrie’s classical account. The reason explains how reward could have an observable effect without serving as the necessary strengthening mechanism: it can end or alter the situation and reduce opportunities for a competing response to become associated.

optWhy.A: A is correct: the stated indirect role makes reinforcement unnecessary as the proposed learning mechanism.
optWhy.B: B misses the explanatory connection between protection and the non-essential status of reinforcement.
optWhy.C: C wrongly denies Guthrie’s context-changing interpretation.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly attributes an essential reinforcement requirement to Guthrie.

key: Reward as protection rather than essential stamping-in

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: In Hull’s system, a response near threshold can occur on some trials and fail to occur on others despite stable nominal training and drive.
reason: The oscillation term represents moment-to-moment variation affecting effective reaction potential.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: Both statements are true within Hull’s model. The reason explains how momentary variation can move effective potential above or below a response threshold without requiring a different habit strength on every trial. It is a theoretical account, not proof that all variability has this cause.

optWhy.A: A is correct: oscillation can alter whether effective potential crosses threshold.
optWhy.B: B incorrectly treats the variation as unrelated to threshold crossings.
optWhy.C: C wrongly denies the role of an oscillation term.
optWhy.D: D wrongly assumes that stable nominal conditions make variable responses impossible.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: The threshold method can present a habit cue at an initially weak intensity and increase it gradually without evoking the old response.
reason: The threshold method requires exhausting the person by repeated performance of the unwanted response.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true of Guthrie’s threshold method: the cue is introduced below the level that elicits the unwanted movement and increased gradually. The reason describes fatigue rather than threshold. These are historical theoretical methods, not a general treatment prescription.

optWhy.A: A wrongly treats exhaustion as defining the threshold method.
optWhy.B: B also assumes the false reason is true.
optWhy.C: C is correct: gradual subthreshold cue presentation differs from fatigue.
optWhy.D: D reverses the truth values.

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: Effect concerns consequences; the original exercise law emphasised use and disuse; readiness concerns the state of the action tendency and the effects of fulfilling or thwarting it; the identical-elements view relates transfer to shared components.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Consequences influence strengthening of a situation–response connection), not a; 2 should match d (Use and disuse were originally proposed to strengthen and weaken connections), not b; 4 should match a (Transfer depends partly on shared elements across learning and test situations), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 2 should match d (Use and disuse were originally proposed to strengthen and weaken connections), not a; 3 should match c (A prepared response tendency and its fulfilment or obstruction matter), not d; 4 should match a (Transfer depends partly on shared elements across learning and test situations), not c.
optWhy.C: Correct: 1–b (Law of effect: Consequences influence strengthening of a situation–response connection); 2–d (Original law of exercise: Use and disuse were originally proposed to strengthen and weaken connections); 3–c (Law of readiness: A prepared response tendency and its fulfilment or obstruction matter); 4–a (Identical elements view of transfer: Transfer depends partly on shared elements across learning and test situations).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Consequences influence strengthening of a situation–response connection), not d; 2 should match d (Use and disuse were originally proposed to strengthen and weaken connections), not c; 3 should match c (A prepared response tendency and its fulfilment or obstruction matter), not b.

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: Habit strength is the learning variable; drive and incentive are distinct motivational influences; stimulus-intensity dynamism concerns the energising effect of cue intensity. Later formulations explicitly incorporated incentive and stimulus intensity.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Learned strength of a stimulus–response tendency associated with reinforcement history), not a; 2 should match c (Motivational effect associated with deprivation or need), not b; 3 should match d (Motivational effect associated with properties of the goal or reward), not c; 4 should match a (Energising influence associated with the intensity of a cue), not d.
optWhy.B: Correct: 1–b (Habit strength: Learned strength of a stimulus–response tendency associated with reinforcement history); 2–c (Drive: Motivational effect associated with deprivation or need); 3–d (Incentive motivation: Motivational effect associated with properties of the goal or reward); 4–a (Stimulus-intensity dynamism: Energising influence associated with the intensity of a cue).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 2 should match c (Motivational effect associated with deprivation or need), not a; 4 should match a (Energising influence associated with the intensity of a cue), not c.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Learned strength of a stimulus–response tendency associated with reinforcement history), not d; 3 should match d (Motivational effect associated with properties of the goal or reward), not b.

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: Threshold begins with a weak cue; fatigue uses repeated responding until the old response ceases; incompatible-response methods arrange another response in the cue’s presence; movement-produced stimuli can link successive movements. These are theoretical descriptions, not blanket clinical recommendations.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match c (Initial cue intensity is kept too weak to evoke the unwanted response and then increased gradually), not a; 2 should match a (Repeated evocation until the old movement no longer occurs and another response can be associated), not b; 3 should match d (The habit cue is present while a response incompatible with the habit is made), not c; 4 should match b (A cue generated by one movement that can occasion the next movement), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 should match c (Initial cue intensity is kept too weak to evoke the unwanted response and then increased gradually), not b; 4 should match b (A cue generated by one movement that can occasion the next movement), not c.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 2 should match a (Repeated evocation until the old movement no longer occurs and another response can be associated), not d; 3 should match d (The habit cue is present while a response incompatible with the habit is made), not a.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–c (Threshold method: Initial cue intensity is kept too weak to evoke the unwanted response and then increased gradually); 2–a (Fatigue method: Repeated evocation until the old movement no longer occurs and another response can be associated); 3–d (Incompatible-response method: The habit cue is present while a response incompatible with the habit is made); 4–b (Movement-produced stimulus: A cue generated by one movement that can occasion the next movement).

key: Guthrie’s habit-breaking methods and movement cues

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: Spread of effect concerns an effect extending beyond the immediately rewarded connection; associative shifting transfers control towards a new cue; belongingness concerns how readily compatible elements connect; identical elements concern overlap between learning and transfer situations.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match c (A consequence can influence nearby associations as well as the immediately associated one), not a; 2 should match a (A response comes under control of a new cue introduced with the original cue), not b; 3 should match d (Some connections are easier to form because their elements fit together meaningfully), not c; 4 should match b (Learning or transfer is aided when elements are shared across situations), not d.
optWhy.B: Correct: 1–c (Spread of effect: A consequence can influence nearby associations as well as the immediately associated one); 2–a (Associative shifting: A response comes under control of a new cue introduced with the original cue); 3–d (Belongingness: Some connections are easier to form because their elements fit together meaningfully); 4–b (Identical-elements transfer: Learning or transfer is aided when elements are shared across situations).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 should match c (A consequence can influence nearby associations as well as the immediately associated one), not b; 4 should match b (Learning or transfer is aided when elements are shared across situations), not c.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 should match c (A consequence can influence nearby associations as well as the immediately associated one), not d; 2 should match a (A response comes under control of a new cue introduced with the original cue), not c; 3 should match d (Some connections are easier to form because their elements fit together meaningfully), not b; 4 should match b (Learning or transfer is aided when elements are shared across situations), not a.

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: Reactive inhibition is linked to the work of responding; conditioned inhibition involves learned inhibitory tendencies; oscillation introduces momentary variability; a fractional anticipatory goal response is a conditioned partial goal response that can generate further stimuli.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match d (Temporary inhibitory influence associated with the work of responding), not a; 2 should match a (Conditioned inhibition associated with cues accompanying response cessation), not b; 3 should match b (Momentary variation in effective response tendency), not c; 4 should match c (A partial goal-related response elicited in advance of the goal), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 should match d (Temporary inhibitory influence associated with the work of responding), not b; 3 should match b (Momentary variation in effective response tendency), not c; 4 should match c (A partial goal-related response elicited in advance of the goal), not d.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 2 should match a (Conditioned inhibition associated with cues accompanying response cessation), not c; 4 should match c (A partial goal-related response elicited in advance of the goal), not a.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–d (Reactive inhibition: Temporary inhibitory influence associated with the work of responding); 2–a (Conditioned inhibition: Conditioned inhibition associated with cues accompanying response cessation); 3–b (Oscillation effect: Momentary variation in effective response tendency); 4–c (Fractional anticipatory goal response: A partial goal-related response elicited in advance of the goal).

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true in the original formulation. 2 is true: use and disuse were emphasised. 3 is false: Thorndike later questioned symmetry between reward and punishment. 4 is true: he revised the importance assigned to exercise alone.

optWhy.A: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2, 4.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3.

key: Historical revisions of effect and exercise

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: a learned association and motivational drive are different constructs. 2 is true of later Hullian formulations. 3 is true: inhibition can oppose response potential. 4 is false: low drive, inhibition or threshold factors can conceal an established habit.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.D: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 3.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: contiguity is the central principle. 2 is true: complex acts contain many specific associations. 3 is false: Guthrie did not require reinforcement for every association. 4 is true: practice can sample new stimulus–movement combinations.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2.

key: One-trial learning without complete one-trial mastery

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true as the basic experimental distinction; the two forms can interact. 2 is false: different individual trajectories or changing stimulus sampling can produce a gradual average. 3 is true: Hull separated habit and performance variables. 4 is false: one study cannot support a universal claim about reinforcement.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 2.
optWhy.B: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 3.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 2, 4 and omits true statement(s) 1, 3.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true as a qualified description of Hull’s classical drive-reduction account. 2 is true: learned associations can confer secondary reinforcing properties. 3 is false: secondary reinforcement depends on a learning history. 4 is false: reinforcer status and incentive motivation are distinct theoretical concepts.

optWhy.A: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3, 4 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3, 4.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true of the threshold method. 2 is false: fatigue and incompatible-response methods differ and neither is defined by a weak cue. 3 is true: an alternative movement is arranged with the cue. 4 is true: the contiguity account concerns a new cue–movement association.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 2 and omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 2 and omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.C: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 3, 4.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 2 and omits true statement(s) 1.

stem: Across repeated puzzle-box trials, a cat makes fewer ineffective movements and opens the latch sooner. A student claims that the curve proves a sudden insight on the first trial. Which evaluation is best?

options.text: A gradual performance pattern is consistent with Thorndike’s trial-and-error account; the curve alone does not prove the claimed sudden insight.
The curve proves that every single trial must improve without exception.
The result shows that consequences cannot influence behaviour.
The cat’s later performance cannot be measured by escape latency.

why: Thorndike interpreted decreasing escape latency and fewer ineffective movements as consistent with selection of effective responses. A fluctuating curve is not a direct record of a hidden learning mechanism and does not logically prove or disprove all possible insight.

optWhy.A: A correctly identifies the compatible account and limits inference from the curve.
optWhy.B: B mistakes a general trend for monotonic improvement on every trial.
optWhy.C: C contradicts the consequence-based account without evidence.
optWhy.D: D rejects a standard observable performance measure.

key: Trial-and-error learning versus claims of insight

stem: After identical reinforced maze training, two groups are tested at the same deprivation level. They encounter the same cues, but one group is signalled a larger food reward. In a later Hullian formulation, which variable is most directly manipulated?

options.text: Habit strength, because an expected reward-size change necessarily changes all prior training.
Incentive motivation, with drive and established training history intended to be held constant.
Reactive inhibition, because the reward is larger.
Primary drive, because any change in reward size is a change in deprivation.

why: In later Hullian theory, the motivational influence of goal magnitude is represented by incentive K, distinct from drive D and habit strength. Matching deprivation and training supports this interpretation, but a real study must still check actual expectations and other differences.

optWhy.A: A treats the new test incentive as an automatic change in prior habit strength.
optWhy.B: B correctly identifies the manipulated goal-related incentive.
optWhy.C: C introduces an inhibitory mechanism not implied by the manipulation.
optWhy.D: D confuses anticipated reward magnitude with deprivation.

stem: A researcher wants to test whether a specific cue–movement association shows further improvement with repeated pairings beyond one pairing, without making reward a programmed consequence. Which design provides the strongest initial comparison?

options.text: Give one group one pairing and a food reward, and another group many pairings with no reward.
Compare a trained group with an untested group that has never encountered the cue.
Use separate groups given one versus several cue–movement pairings without programmed reward, match cue and motor exposure as closely as possible, and test all groups under the same conditions.
Give both groups the same training but change the test cue only for the one-pairing group.

why: A one-versus-several pairing comparison, with equivalent testing and controls for cue and motor exposure, targets the number of pairings while avoiding a programmed reward confound. Unprogrammed consequences, pre-existing response biases and the possibility that tests alter associations still require control; no design automatically proves a theory.

optWhy.A: A confounds pairing number with reward.
optWhy.B: B does not isolate the effect of pairing number from exposure and testing.
optWhy.C: C best controls the main alternatives while directly contrasting one and several pairings.
optWhy.D: D confounds training amount with test-cue generalisation.

stem: A rat learns to press a lever for food during acquisition. Lever pressing then declines across extinction sessions in which food is withheld. After a delay, some pressing returns at the start of a test in the same apparatus without food. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: Extinction proves that the original learning was permanently erased, so returning responses are impossible.
The returning response is compatible with spontaneous recovery; extinction reduced performance but does not by itself prove erasure of the original learning.
The delay demonstrates new food reinforcement during the test.
A decline during extinction proves that the rat never acquired the lever response.

why: Acquisition establishes the response under reinforcement; extinction involves withholding the previously arranged outcome and observing a decline. Return after a delay is compatible with spontaneous recovery and indicates that extinction performance alone cannot establish erasure. Retention is assessed through later behaviour, which can reflect both original and extinction learning.

optWhy.A: A makes an erasure claim incompatible with the described return.
optWhy.B: B correctly interprets recovery while recognising the limits of a performance measure.
optWhy.C: C invents reinforcement despite its explicit absence.
optWhy.D: D ignores the acquired response observed before extinction.

stem: A person notices that seeing a particular desk light on is a cue for nail biting. During a planned exercise, the light is on while the person places both hands flat on the table, making nail biting at that moment impossible. In Guthrie’s terminology, what method is illustrated?

options.text: Fatigue, because biting is continued until exhaustion.
Associative shifting, because reward magnitude is changed.
Threshold, because the cue is gradually intensified from below its response threshold.
Incompatible response, because a competing movement occurs in the presence of the habit cue.

why: The example arranges an alternative movement that is incompatible with the unwanted response while the cue is present. Guthrie’s interpretation is that the relevant stimulus pattern becomes associated with the new movement. A single example is not evidence of clinical effectiveness.

optWhy.A: A describes repeated unwanted responding, which is not the procedure.
optWhy.B: B changes neither reward magnitude nor control to a new cue.
optWhy.C: C requires a gradual cue-intensity manipulation not described here.
optWhy.D: D correctly identifies an incompatible movement paired with the cue.

stem: Two animals receive the same reinforced training. At test, one is sated and responds more slowly than the deprived animal. Which follow-up would best investigate whether the speed difference reflects motivational performance factors rather than a training difference?

options.text: Compare their speeds only in the original different motivational states.
Give additional unequal training before measuring either animal again.
Test both animals under the same deprivation and incentive conditions, using equivalent cues and appropriate counterbalancing.
Conclude that the slower animal has no learned habit because it responded slowly.

why: A common-condition test reduces the immediate drive and incentive difference and helps assess whether the performance gap persists. Equivalent cues and counterbalancing reduce alternative explanations. Even then, the observed response is an indirect measure and cannot establish identical latent habits with certainty.

optWhy.A: A preserves the motivational confound.
optWhy.B: B adds unequal learning histories.
optWhy.C: C standardises major performance factors before comparison.
optWhy.D: D infers complete absence of learning from one slow performance.

key: Testing latent learning separately from motivation

stem: In a Hullian analysis, a cue near a maze goal comes to evoke a small part of the animal’s eating response before food is reached; the response itself produces internal stimulation. Which sequence best represents the proposed mechanism?

options.text: Cue → complete unlearned eating of absent food → no further stimulation.
Cue → fractional anticipatory goal response → response-produced goal stimuli that can influence subsequent behaviour.
Cue → punishment → permanent elimination of all drive.
Cue → retinal disparity → immediate extinction of the maze habit.

why: Hull proposed that cues preceding a goal could evoke a fractional anticipatory goal response, conventionally rG. That response produces internal stimuli, sG, which can contribute to the organisation and motivation of later behaviour. This is a historical theoretical mechanism, not an observed fact in the hypothetical case.

optWhy.A: A replaces a fractional conditioned response with complete consumption of absent food.
optWhy.B: B correctly orders the cue, partial response and response-produced stimuli.
optWhy.C: C substitutes punishment and an unsupported permanent drive change.
optWhy.D: D introduces an unrelated perceptual cue and extinction.

stem: For this question only, use an illustrative simplified Hullian performance equation P=(H×D×K×V)-I. A response occurs when P exceeds 0.30; there is no oscillation. Let H=0.8, D=0.5, V=1 and I=0.2. If K changes from 1 to 2 while all other values remain fixed, which prediction follows from this stipulated model?

options.text: P changes from 0.4 to 0.8, so the response occurs in both conditions.
P changes from 0.2 to 0.6, so the response crosses threshold without changing H.
P changes from 0.2 to 0.6, proving H doubled.
P remains 0.2 because incentive cannot affect performance.

why: With K=1, P=(0.8×0.5×1×1)−0.2=0.2, below threshold. With K=2, P=(0.8×0.5×2×1)−0.2=0.6, above threshold. H is fixed; the example illustrates a modelled performance change, not a verbatim statement of every version of Hull’s system.

optWhy.A: A omits the stipulated inhibitory subtraction.
optWhy.B: B correctly computes both potentials and distinguishes the fixed habit from the incentive change.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly changes H even though it is stipulated as constant.
optWhy.D: D ignores K’s multiplicative role in the provided equation.

key: Incentive, inhibition and a response threshold

stem: A tone precedes food regardless of what a dog does; in another procedure, a lever press produces food. Which comparison best describes the programmed relationships?

options.text: Both procedures make food contingent on lever pressing.
The first arranges a stimulus–stimulus relationship; the second makes an outcome contingent on a response.
The tone is necessarily a discriminative stimulus, not a conditioned stimulus.
Classical responses must be involuntary and operant responses always conscious.

why: The first procedure arranges tone–food pairing independently of the target response; the second arranges a press–food consequence. Respondent and operant processes can coexist, and voluntary versus involuntary is an imperfect distinction.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly assigns the operant contingency to both arrangements.
optWhy.B: B identifies the programmed event–event and response–outcome relations.
optWhy.C: C ignores that the tone predicts food regardless of responding.
optWhy.D: D makes absolute claims about awareness and voluntariness.

key: Procedural distinction between classical and operant conditioning

stem: Two groups experience the same proportion of tone presentations followed by shock within equal observation windows. Group 1 rarely receives shock outside the tone; Group 2 receives shock just as often outside the tone as during it. Which prediction best reflects Rescorla’s contingency analysis?

options.text: The tone should be more informative in Group 1 and generally support stronger fear conditioning, other things equal.
Both groups must show identical fear because their tone–shock pairings are equal.
The tone is necessarily a conditioned inhibitor in both groups.
Group 2 must show stronger fear because background shock provides more pairings with the tone.

why: Group 1 has positive contingency: shock is more likely during than outside the tone. In Group 2 the probabilities are equal, so the tone adds little information. Contiguity and background events both matter; the prediction is not a universal quantitative law.

optWhy.A: A correctly compares differential predictive information.
optWhy.B: B neglects shock outside the cue.
optWhy.C: C mistakes positive and zero contingencies for necessarily inhibitory arrangements.
optWhy.D: D confuses unsignalled shocks with extra tone–shock pairings.

stem: In experiment 1, cue A is paired with food before compound AX is paired with food. In experiment 2, a salient cue B and a weaker cue X are paired with food as a compound from the outset, with no pretraining. Appropriate controls show reduced responding to X in each case. Which interpretation fits?

options.text: Both effects are latent inhibition because X was pre-exposed alone without food.
Experiment 1 illustrates blocking; experiment 2 illustrates overshadowing.
Experiment 1 illustrates overshadowing; experiment 2 illustrates blocking.
Both effects prove that X was never contiguous with food.

why: Blocking is reduced learning about X after A has already predicted the outcome. Overshadowing is reduced responding to X after compound training with a more salient cue, compared with an appropriate X-alone control. Competing mechanisms and test performance should be considered.

optWhy.A: A invents unreinforced X pre-exposure.
optWhy.B: B correctly distinguishes prior predictor training from initial compound competition.
optWhy.C: C reverses the procedures.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly denies compound–food pairings.

key: Prior prediction versus competition within a novel compound

stem: A cumulative response record shows pauses immediately after each reinforcer followed by accelerating responding as a constant time since reinforcement elapses. A second record shows high, relatively steady responding, with reinforcers after varying response counts. Which pair best fits, if contingency logs agree?
why: The first pattern is characteristic of an FI schedule, in which the first response after a fixed interval is reinforced; the second is compatible with VR, defined by varying response requirements. Patterns are tendencies, not definitive identification without contingency records.

optWhy.A: A reverses time and response-count relations.
optWhy.B: B fails to match the characteristic FI scallop and VR response requirement.
optWhy.C: C correctly matches the temporal scallop and variable response counts.
optWhy.D: D ignores the fixed elapsed time and variable ratio.

stem: In baseline a child freely chooses 20 minutes of drawing and 5 minutes of reading in an hour. Later, drawing is restricted below baseline and made available only after reading. Reading increases. Which interpretation is most defensible?

options.text: Drawing cannot reinforce reading because neither is a primary reinforcer.
The result is consistent with Premack’s relative-probability account and also with response-deprivation theory; separate manipulations are needed to distinguish them.
The outcome is punishment because access to drawing was restricted.
The result proves the same drawing contingency would increase reading for every child.

why: The more frequent baseline activity, drawing, is contingent on reading, consistent with Premack. Restricting drawing below its baseline level also fits response deprivation. Because both predict the outcome here, a test varying baseline preference and restriction independently is needed.

optWhy.A: A wrongly excludes activities as reinforcers.
optWhy.B: B recognises overlapping predictions and the need for a discriminating test.
optWhy.C: C ignores the observed increase in the target response following contingent access.
optWhy.D: D overgeneralises across individuals and conditions.

key: Overlapping predictions of Premack and response deprivation

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A decrease in a conditioned response during extinction need not mean the original association has been permanently erased.
reason: After extinction, responding can return with time or a context change without renewed CS–US pairings.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true: recovery and context effects show that low responding does not necessarily imply erasure. The reason is true: such recovery provides evidence that the original learning need not have been permanently erased, although it does not establish exactly how extinction is stored.

optWhy.A: A correctly connects recovery without retraining to the qualified assertion.
optWhy.B: B overlooks the relevance of recovery without retraining.
optWhy.C: C wrongly denies documented post-extinction recovery.
optWhy.D: D wrongly asserts that extinction must erase the original learning.

key: Extinction as new learning rather than mere forgetting

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: In a trace-conditioning procedure, the CS terminates before the US begins.
reason: The CS–US-free trace interval between CS offset and US onset differentiates trace from standard delay conditioning, in which the CS remains present when the US begins.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true: the CS ends before the US begins. The reason is true and explains that the temporal gap distinguishes trace from standard delay conditioning. The intervening contextual stimulation is not literally absent; the gap is free of the specified CS and US.

optWhy.A: A correctly states the defining temporal distinction.
optWhy.B: B misses the explanatory relevance of the gap.
optWhy.C: C wrongly denies the trace-versus-delay distinction.
optWhy.D: D wrongly denies that the CS ends first.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A new cue may elicit a conditioned response after it is paired with an established excitatory CS, even when the US is not presented during that phase.
reason: In second-order conditioning the previously trained CS can serve as the Pavlovian reinforcing event for conditioning the new cue.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true as a description of second-order conditioning under suitable conditions. The reason is true and explains the use of an established CS in place of the US during the second stage; the effect depends on procedure and is often weaker than first-order conditioning.

optWhy.A: A correctly links the established CS to second-order learning.
optWhy.B: B overlooks the explanatory link.
optWhy.C: C wrongly denies the functional role of the established CS.
optWhy.D: D wrongly rules out second-order conditioning.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Latent inhibition and extinction are identical because both require prior reinforced CS–US training before CS-alone presentations.
reason: In a latent-inhibition procedure, pre-exposure to the target cue without the US can slow its later acquisition compared with a suitably controlled cue.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is false: latent inhibition commonly involves unreinforced pre-exposure before acquisition, whereas extinction usually follows established conditioning. The reason is true, subject to appropriate controls for exposure and testing.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly accepts identical training histories.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A cue trained as a conditioned inhibitor can be assessed by asking whether it reduces responding to a separately trained excitor in a summation test.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
