stem: A dog initially salivates to food but not to a neutral tone. The tone is repeatedly presented just before food, independently of the dog’s behaviour. Later the tone alone elicits salivation. Which assignment is correct?

options.text: Tone = UCS; food = CS; salivation to food = CR.
Food = UCS; salivation to food = UCR; tone after training = CS; salivation to tone = CR.
Food = discriminative stimulus; the dog’s salivation produces the food.
Tone = operant response; salivation = primary reinforcer.

why: Food is the unconditioned stimulus and salivation to food the UCR. After acquisition, the tone is the CS and salivation to the tone the CR. The CR need not be biologically identical in every feature to the UCR.

optWhy.A: A reverses cue and unconditioned event.
optWhy.B: B correctly identifies all four components.
optWhy.C: C invents a response–food contingency absent from the procedure.
optWhy.D: D confuses stimuli, responses and consequences.

key: Identifying CS, US, CR and UR

stem: A tone originally predicts food and evokes salivation. After repeated tone-alone extinction trials, salivation becomes minimal. The next day, before any new tone–food pairings, the tone elicits some salivation. What best explains the observation?

options.text: Reacquisition due to new tone–food pairings.
Proof that extinction never changed the animal’s behaviour.
Spontaneous recovery after a rest interval, consistent with persistence of some original learning.
Instrumental reinforcement of salivation by new food delivery.

why: The return of responding after a delay without renewed pairing is spontaneous recovery, not reacquisition. Extinction reduced responding, but its effect need not mean that the original learning was erased. Recovery need not restore the original response fully.

optWhy.A: A requires renewed CS–US training, explicitly absent.
optWhy.B: B contradicts the reported decline during extinction.
optWhy.C: C matches response return after rest with no new training.
optWhy.D: D invents food delivery contingent on salivation.

stem: In a hypothetical, ethically approved assessment, a child repeatedly hears a brief startling sound immediately after seeing a previously neutral toy; later the toy alone evokes distress. A second child only watches a peer react fearfully to the toy, with no sound or other direct pairing. Which comparison is most defensible?

options.text: Both must have acquired fear through identical direct CS–US pairings.
The first pattern is compatible with a conditioned emotional response; the second could involve observational learning, subject to controls for prior experience and other cues.
The toy is the US in the first case because it was initially neutral.
Distress to the toy proves the child cannot generalise fear to similar cues.

why: The first arrangement resembles Watson and Rayner’s conditioned-emotion logic: toy CS, startling sound US, and later distress to the toy a CR. The second involves modelling rather than the stated direct pairing. Neither observation alone rules out prior experience, contextual cues or other influences.

optWhy.A: A invents a direct aversive pairing for the observer.
optWhy.B: B distinguishes the procedures and retains appropriate inferential caution.
optWhy.C: C mislabels the initially neutral cue as the US.
optWhy.D: D draws an unsupported conclusion about generalisation.

key: Direct conditioned fear versus observational learning

stem: In a classroom, a green card signals that a raised hand will receive teacher attention; with a red card, raised hands are not followed by attention. Hand-raising becomes much more frequent under green. Which analysis best identifies the green card?

options.text: A discriminative stimulus for an operant response because it signals the attention contingency.
An unconditioned reinforcer because it is presented before the response.
A conditioned response because it follows hand-raising.
The sole proof that hand-raising is a Pavlovian reflex independent of consequences.

why: The antecedent green card signals when the behaviour, hand-raising, is followed by attention; differential responding shows stimulus control. Attention functions as a reinforcer only if the contingency increases future hand-raising. The card may acquire other functions, but its signalled availability role is discriminative.

optWhy.A: A correctly identifies antecedent, response and consequence relation.
optWhy.B: B confuses an antecedent with an unconditioned consequence.
optWhy.C: C misclassifies the card as a response and reverses its position.
optWhy.D: D ignores the response-dependent attention contingency.

stem: A teacher initially provides contingent praise for any attempt to speak in a group, then reinforces audible single words, then short sentences. Each newly reinforced form increases before the criterion is raised. What procedure is most directly illustrated?

options.text: Chaining, because the teacher reinforces a fixed sequence of different steps.
Extinction alone, because no responses receive consequences.
Shaping by differential reinforcement of successive approximations to a target response.
Classical delay conditioning, because praise is presented regardless of behaviour.

why: The teacher changes the response criterion gradually and differentially reinforces closer approximations to speaking in sentences. This is shaping, not necessarily the chaining of multiple response components. The observed increases support praise functioning as reinforcement under the arrangement. To assess generalisation and maintenance, monitor speaking across people and settings after support is gradually faded.

optWhy.A: A requires a linked sequence of component responses, not just improved response form.
optWhy.B: B ignores contingent praise.
optWhy.C: C correctly identifies successive approximations and their observed increase.
optWhy.D: D falsely removes the response–consequence contingency.

sub: Variable ratio and resistance to extinction
stem: On a gambling-like task, monetary payouts follow an unpredictable number of responses, averaging 20; the payouts increase future responding. The participant responds at a high, relatively steady rate and continues for some time when payouts are discontinued. Which account best fits the programmed schedule?

options.text: FI 20, because reinforcement depends on 20 minutes.
FR 20, because exactly 20 responses are required every time.
VI 20, because each reinforcer depends on varying elapsed intervals.
VR 20, because the response requirement varies around a mean of 20; persistence is compatible with a partial-reinforcement effect.

why: VR 20 specifies a varying response count with an average requirement of 20. High, fairly steady response rates and persistence during extinction are common tendencies, not guarantees for every gambler or arrangement. Programmed contingencies, not persistence alone, identify the schedule.

optWhy.A: A substitutes a fixed time criterion for a variable response count.
optWhy.B: B wrongly makes every requirement exactly 20.
optWhy.C: C substitutes variable time for variable response count.
optWhy.D: D matches the programmed ratio and qualified persistence pattern.

stem: An employee receives an earned bonus immediately after every tenth completed task, and the count then restarts. Records show a short pause after bonuses followed by rapid work. Which interpretation fits the stated contingency and pattern?

options.text: Fixed interval 10: the first task after ten minutes is reinforced.
Fixed ratio 10: every tenth response produces the bonus; a post-reinforcement pause is common but not inevitable.
Variable ratio 10: the required task count changes unpredictably.
Continuous reinforcement: every completed task produces a bonus.

why: The fixed response count makes this FR 10. Post-reinforcement pausing and high rates are common ratio patterns, though their size depends on the conditions. Whether the bonus actually reinforces work is established by its effect on subsequent work, not by its label.

optWhy.A: A substitutes elapsed time for a fixed task count.
optWhy.B: B identifies the contingency and qualifies the characteristic pattern.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly makes the task count variable.
optWhy.D: D wrongly claims every individual task is followed by a bonus.

key: Fixed ratio identified by response requirement

stem: A patient consumes a novel drink before a medical treatment and becomes nauseated several hours later. On a later occasion, the patient avoids that flavour. No aversive event immediately followed the drink. Which conclusion best integrates conditioning evidence and its limits?

options.text: The delay makes a learned taste aversion impossible, because all CS–US intervals must be seconds long.
The flavour is necessarily a generalised conditioned reinforcer.

The aversion is compatible with taste–illness learning across a long delay; alternative causes need consideration, and cue–outcome learning is biologically constrained rather than uniformly equipotential.
The avoidance proves every visual or auditory cue present was learned equally strongly.

why: A novel flavour followed by delayed illness can support conditioned taste aversion, as long-delay and cue–consequence research illustrates. The vignette is compatible with, not proof of, this mechanism: prior dislike, context, information and other causes require assessment. The outcome challenges simple equipotentiality, not all associative learning.

optWhy.A: A wrongly assumes all effective conditioning requires a very short interval.
optWhy.B: B confuses a potential taste CS with a conditioned reinforcer.
optWhy.C: C incorporates long-delay learning, selective associations and inferential limits.
optWhy.D: D assumes equal learning across modalities despite evidence for cue–outcome selectivity.

key: Taste aversion, delay and biological preparedness

stem: A researcher labels sensory registers, a short-term store and a long-term store as structures, while treating rehearsal and retrieval strategies as operations. Which account best fits this distinction?

options.text: Atkinson–Shiffrin distinguished structural components from control processes; later research shows that this framework is not an exhaustive account.
Rehearsal is necessarily a separate sensory register.
The framework implies that every memory must be verbally rehearsed to reach long-term storage.
Working memory consists only of an undifferentiated passive register.

why: The multistore model distinguished structural stores from control processes such as rehearsal and retrieval. Subsequent evidence for multiple working-memory components and multiple long-term systems limits any claim that the model is exhaustive.

optWhy.A: A correctly identifies the distinction and its scope.
optWhy.B: B mistakes a process for a structural sensory register.
optWhy.C: C makes an unwarranted universal claim about verbal rehearsal.
optWhy.D: D mischaracterises working memory and ignores later component evidence.

stem: Immediately after hearing a list, participants recall early and late words especially well. In a separate condition, a demanding distractor is inserted after the list and before free recall. Which change is most consistent with the classic account?

options.text: The distractor should selectively remove all evidence of semantic memory.
The distractor can reduce the recency advantage, while early-item recall may be less affected; these patterns do not prove two exclusive stores.
The distractor must improve recency because the last items are rehearsed during it.
Primacy and recency must always change identically because they reflect the same retrieval condition.

why: In classic serial-position experiments, immediate recency is often reduced by a filled retention interval, while primacy can be less affected. Primacy is often linked to rehearsal and durable encoding and recency to temporal distinctiveness or accessible recent information; neither pattern uniquely proves a particular architecture.

optWhy.A: A asserts a global semantic deficit not implied by the manipulation.
optWhy.B: B gives the expected qualified dissociation without overclaiming mechanism.
optWhy.C: C ignores that a demanding distractor competes with maintenance.
optWhy.D: D assumes an invariance not supported by the comparison.

key: Primacy and recency under delayed recall

stem: A chess expert recalls a meaningful board position better than a novice but not a random arrangement with the same number of pieces. Which interpretation best reconciles chunking with differing capacity estimates?

options.text: Expertise increases the number of independent raw items that can always be held without limit.
The difference proves that all people have exactly seven unchanging slots.
Familiar configurations can be encoded as meaningful chunks; estimates such as Miller’s seven and Cowan’s roughly four depend on units and task conditions.
The novice has no sensory memory for chess pieces.

why: Knowledge can group multiple pieces into familiar patterns, increasing the amount of material represented without establishing unlimited capacity. Miller’s rough 7±2 summary and Cowan’s approximately four chunks under controlled conditions concern different operational constraints and are not universal constants.

optWhy.A: A assumes unlimited capacity and ignores random-position performance.
optWhy.B: B treats a historical estimate as an exact universal limit.
optWhy.C: C correctly invokes knowledge-dependent recoding and conditional estimates.
optWhy.D: D infers absence of sensory registration without evidence.

stem: Participants learn several categories of exemplars. They practise retrieving half the exemplars from some categories, then take a final recall test. Unpractised exemplars from practised categories are recalled less well than comparable exemplars from untouched categories. Which inference is best?

options.text: The pattern is consistent with retrieval-induced forgetting of related competitors, but its mechanism requires further tests.
All memories have been erased by the final test.
The practice must have improved every unpractised exemplar.
The untouched categories are the retrieval-practised items.

why: The critical comparison is between unpractised items from practised categories and baseline items from unpractised categories. A disadvantage for the former is retrieval-induced forgetting; inhibition and other accounts require careful controls and are not uniquely established by this pattern alone.

optWhy.A: A identifies the appropriate contrast and avoids claiming a unique mechanism.
optWhy.B: B overstates a relative recall decrement as complete erasure.
optWhy.C: C reverses the stated result.
optWhy.D: D confuses the baseline with the practised subset.

key: Retrieval practice can affect related competitors

stem: Two groups study the same words, one making semantic judgments and the other judging rhyme. At test, semantic study is better for meaning-based recall, but rhyme study can be better on a rhyme-cued test. Which interpretation is strongest?

options.text: Semantic processing must win on every possible test.
Neither encoding condition affects later performance.
The pattern supports transfer-appropriate processing: compatibility between study operations and test demands can modify the usual depth advantage.
The rhyme condition demonstrates that recognition never depends on meaning.

why: Semantic processing often benefits many later tests, as levels-of-processing research emphasises, but retrieval depends on how encoding operations match test demands. A rhyme-cued test can favour rhyme processing; depth, distinctiveness and elaboration do not imply an invariant rank ordering for every task.

optWhy.A: A makes depth an exceptionless rule.
optWhy.B: B contradicts both described differences.
optWhy.C: C appropriately integrates processing depth with study–test fit.
optWhy.D: D makes an unsupported universal claim about recognition.

stem: A 12-letter display has three rows of four. In whole report a participant names four letters. With an immediate, unpredictable post-display cue to report one row, the participant averages three correct letters from the cued row. Assuming comparable accuracy across rows, what is the estimated availability across the display?

options.text: Three letters, because only the reported row ever existed in the visual system.
Nine letters, estimated by multiplying three reported letters by three possible rows; this does not mean nine were all reported on one trial.
Twelve letters with certainty, because partial report is error-free.
Four letters, because whole report always measures all information initially available.

why: Three correct items per row times three equally cued rows gives an estimated nine initially available items. This is an extrapolation across possible cued rows, not nine letters actually reported together. A delayed cue typically reduces the advantage, and performance depends on display and masking conditions.

optWhy.A: A confuses the sampled subset with the full display’s estimated availability.
optWhy.B: B calculates 3×3 and recognises the inference’s limit.
optWhy.C: C ignores the reported errors and claims certainty.
optWhy.D: D assumes whole report exhaustively measures initial availability.

stem: Students learn a word list in Room A. In a controlled comparison, recall is better in Room A than in Room B, with learning time and testing procedures otherwise matched. Which interpretation is most defensible?

options.text: The result is compatible with context-dependent retrieval cues, but does not prove that learning in Room B is impossible.
The change in room necessarily erased all stored representations.
The effect proves that mood valence and environmental context are identical constructs.
Context can never influence retrieval because memory is a literal recording.

why: Environmental features present at encoding may serve as retrieval cues when reinstated at test, consistent with encoding specificity. The finding is conditional on the materials and design; it does not establish an absolute requirement for the original room.

optWhy.A: A identifies the matching-context interpretation without overgeneralising.
optWhy.B: B wrongly infers erasure from reduced recall.
optWhy.C: C confuses external context with mood-congruent content.
optWhy.D: D assumes an infallible recording model and denies the observation.

stem: A patient with medial temporal lobe damage cannot consciously recall having practised a mirror-tracing task, yet tracing errors decline over several sessions. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: All memory systems are intact because performance improves.
Skill improvement and explicit recollection can dissociate; the pattern alone does not identify a single exclusive brain location for the skill.
The patient consciously remembers each training episode but refuses to report it.
The improvement proves that the medial temporal lobe contributes to no form of memory.

why: Improvement despite impaired conscious recall is consistent with a dissociation between non-declarative skill learning and declarative episodic remembering. Practice, sensory and motor changes must be controlled, and the dissociation does not map a whole skill to one exclusive structure or eliminate other medial temporal functions.

optWhy.A: A ignores the explicit-memory deficit.
optWhy.B: B recognises a selective dissociation and limits anatomical inference.
optWhy.C: C invents deliberate refusal.
optWhy.D: D generalises far beyond the observed dissociation.

stem: A participant normally repeats six visually presented digits in order, but recall drops while continuously saying an irrelevant syllable during presentation and retention. Which interpretation best fits Baddeley’s model?

options.text: Concurrent articulation can disrupt verbal recoding and rehearsal, reducing serial recall; it does not abolish working memory as a whole.
The irrelevant syllable must increase the phonological loop’s available rehearsal capacity.
The result proves the visuospatial sketchpad is the only component of working memory.
The digits were never visually perceived because the participant spoke.

why: Concurrent articulation occupies articulatory processes used for verbal rehearsal and can interfere with recoding visual digits into speech-based form. Performance can also reflect attentional and output demands; the result does not establish that every component of working memory has failed.

optWhy.A: A identifies a plausible component-specific mechanism with suitable caution.
optWhy.B: B reverses the expected effect of suppression.
optWhy.C: C ignores the verbal task and other working-memory components.
optWhy.D: D infers a visual-perception failure that is not demonstrated.

stem: A person accurately recalls a scientific claim encountered last week but attributes it to a teacher when it was actually read online. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The person has no memory for the claim itself.
This is a source-monitoring error: item content is accessible, but its origin is misattributed.
This proves all semantic knowledge is stored as an exact audiovisual recording.
This is necessarily prospective-memory failure rather than an error about a past source.

why: The content and its origin are separable aspects of memory. Correctly recalling a claim while misattributing its source is a source-monitoring error; it does not establish complete loss of item memory or the precise neural mechanism.

optWhy.A: A contradicts correct recall of the claim.
optWhy.B: B correctly distinguishes content memory from source attribution.
optWhy.C: C assumes literal recording despite the source error.
optWhy.D: D misclassifies a past-source error as necessarily a future-intention failure.

stem: A researcher matches short and long words as closely as possible for familiarity and frequency. Immediate serial recall is poorer for long words, and the difference becomes much smaller during concurrent irrelevant articulation. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: The pattern is consistent with a contribution from articulatory rehearsal, but output interference and other explanations require further tests.
Long words are necessarily held in a separate, unlimited long-term store.
The result proves that the phonological similarity effect must disappear in every auditory and visual procedure.
The result shows that the central executive plays no role in any memory task.

why: The long-word disadvantage and its reduction under suppression are compatible with a rehearsal-based interpretation of the word-length effect. However, suppression may also change output or introduce interference; lexical factors and alternative mechanisms require further control. The effect is not an invariant proof of a single mechanism.

optWhy.A: A interprets the interaction cautiously and identifies alternatives.
optWhy.B: B invents a separate unlimited store.
optWhy.C: C overgeneralises across presentation modalities and procedures.
optWhy.D: D draws an unsupported claim about all executive functions.

stem: After studying a list, a participant freely recalls few items but recognises many studied items above a matched false-alarm baseline when presented with old and new words. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: All traces were certainly absent before the recognition test.
Recognition may provide cues that support access not obtained in free recall; the difference alone does not isolate a unique storage or retrieval mechanism.
Recognition and recall must measure exactly the same operations in identical amounts.
The participant has necessarily acquired a new procedural skill.

why: Above-baseline recognition indicates that study influenced later discrimination even though free recall was poor. Recognition supplies test items as cues and imposes different decision demands, so a retrieval-access account is plausible; the comparison alone cannot precisely quantify storage or identify a unique mechanism. Relearning savings can provide another measure of retained influence.

optWhy.A: A conflicts with above-baseline discrimination.
optWhy.B: B recognises cue and task differences without proving a unique cause.
optWhy.C: C ignores distinct cueing and decision demands.
optWhy.D: D invents a skill-learning outcome.

stem: Students study a passage once. One randomly assigned group then practises recalling it repeatedly; another restudies it for the same total time. One week later both take the same unannounced test, and the retrieval-practice group performs better. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: The pattern is consistent with a testing effect under these conditions, although feedback, practice success and task differences can affect its size.
The result proves retrieval practice always outperforms every restudy method at every delay.
The result demonstrates that initial encoding did not occur in either group.
The advantage must be caused by a longer total practice period for the retrieval group.

why: A delayed advantage for retrieval practice over time-matched restudy is consistent with test-enhanced learning. Random assignment and equal practice time strengthen the comparison, but the procedures differ in activities, and feedback, initial success, final test and retention interval can affect outcomes.

optWhy.A: A identifies the testing effect without a universal claim.
optWhy.B: B overgeneralises beyond the tested comparison.
optWhy.C: C ignores the common initial study and subsequent retention.
optWhy.D: D contradicts the stipulated equal total practice time.

stem: A learner originally needs 20 trials to reach a stated mastery criterion for a list. After one week, relearning to the same criterion takes 8 trials. Using savings = (original trials − relearning trials) / original trials × 100, what is the savings score?
why: Savings = (20−8)/20 × 100 = 60%. Relearning requires fewer trials than original learning and is evidence of retained influence even if unaided recall is poor. Savings is a measure of performance, not a direct measurement of trace strength.

optWhy.A: A divides relearning trials by original trials rather than computing savings.
optWhy.B: B correctly calculates the percentage reduction in trials.
optWhy.C: C confuses the trial count with the proportion saved.
