Decay is impossible because the distractor was nonverbal.
The result proves retroactive interference from a separately learned word list, although none was presented.
The longer delay is associated with lower recall, but differences in cumulative distractor processing, rehearsal or temporal context prevent a unique decay inference.

why: Random assignment and a constant task type strengthen the comparison, but a longer interval includes more task cycles and can alter rehearsal and context. The result is compatible with time-dependent loss and interference-based accounts; neither is uniquely established.

optWhy.A: A treats elapsed time as isolated from all correlated processes.
optWhy.B: B assumes nonverbal processing cannot affect verbal retention.
optWhy.C: C invents an interpolated word list.
optWhy.D: D identifies the observed association and the principal remaining confounds.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Freudian repression and deliberate suppression are identical because both necessarily involve conscious intent to keep material out of awareness.
reason: Deliberate suppression involves an intentional effort to avoid a thought; repression was historically proposed as an unconscious defence.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is false and the reason is true as a distinction between definitions. Repression remains empirically debated, and intentional laboratory control of retrieval is not itself proof of Freudian repression.

optWhy.A: A wrongly accepts conscious intent as part of both constructs.
optWhy.B: B also treats the false assertion as true.
optWhy.C: C reverses the truth values.
optWhy.D: D correctly distinguishes intentional suppression from the historical unconscious construct.

sub: Release from proactive interference: baseline design
stem: After three fruit-word lists, a category-shift group receives a tool-word list and recalls more items than a group receiving a fourth fruit list. Which additional control best tests whether release from proactive interference, rather than an inherent difference in list difficulty, contributed?

options.text: Compare the two groups only after giving the shift group more study time.
Counterbalance the specific fruit and tool lists and measure their first-trial recall in independent participants without prior lists.
Remove the no-shift group and test only tool words.
Change the retention interval and category simultaneously.

why: A baseline without preceding lists estimates inherent recall differences, while counterbalancing reduces item-specific confounding. A shift benefit beyond such differences is consistent with release from proactive interference; attention to novelty and other effects of the shift still need examination.

optWhy.A: A introduces a study-time confound.
optWhy.B: B provides list-difficulty baselines and counterbalances specific materials.
optWhy.C: C eliminates the comparison needed to assess the category shift.
optWhy.D: D confounds category with elapsed time.

stem: Match each researcher or research team with the best-associated paradigm or contribution.
why: Bartlett studied reconstruction using an unfamiliar story; Tulving and Thomson developed encoding specificity; Loftus and Palmer manipulated post-event wording; Anderson and Green studied intentional retrieval control. These programmes differ in design and do not imply identical mechanisms.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not a; 2 matches d, not b; 3 matches a, not c; 4 matches c, not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not d; 2 matches d, not a; 3 matches a, not c; 4 matches c, not b.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not c; 4 matches c, not b.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–b, 2–d, 3–a, 4–c.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: knowledge can support encoding yet bias reconstruction. 2 is true as a conditional spacing effect, not a guarantee for every test or spacing schedule. 3 is true by definition, although its benefit depends on controls and outcome. 4 is false: curves vary with conditions. Transfer-appropriate processing also predicts effects of overlap between practice operations and test demands.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.C: Correct: includes all and only true statements.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 2.

stem: After learning cue–target pairs to criterion, participants repeatedly retrieve some targets when cued, avoid thinking of other targets when cued, and receive no intermediate exposure to a third baseline set. On a final test instructing recall of all items, no-think targets are recalled less often than baseline targets. What follows?

options.text: The pattern is compatible with suppression-induced forgetting, but cue-independent probes and controls for substitution and initial learning are needed to investigate mechanisms.
The result proves unconscious Freudian repression of trauma.
The lower score is necessarily caused by lack of initial study because criterion learning was absent.
The no-think instruction itself guarantees identical forgetting in every participant.

why: No-think versus unpractised baseline estimates a potential suppression-related cost rather than merely a benefit for think items. Independent probes, initial-learning checks and strategy controls help assess inhibition and interference alternatives; neither cue independence nor one result proves a unique mechanism or clinical repression.

optWhy.A: A correctly interprets the baseline contrast and limits causal attribution.
optWhy.B: B conflates deliberate laboratory instructions with psychoanalytic trauma claims.
optWhy.C: C contradicts the stated criterion training.
optWhy.D: D treats a group-level possibility as a universal guarantee.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Some reactivated memories can become temporarily susceptible to disruption before subsequent restabilisation.
reason: Every instance of retrieval necessarily destabilises every consolidated memory and requires identical protein synthesis.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true as a qualified reconsolidation claim. The reason is false: susceptibility depends on memory and reactivation conditions, and mechanisms cannot be generalised identically across all memories and species.

optWhy.A: A wrongly accepts the universal claim.
optWhy.B: B also accepts the false reason.
optWhy.C: C correctly distinguishes a conditional finding from a universal law.
optWhy.D: D reverses the truth values.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true as a broad timescale distinction. 2 is true but does not imply that all remote memories become hippocampus-independent. 3 is false: the definition given describes retrograde amnesia; anterograde concerns impaired new learning after onset. 4 is true as a qualified finding.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Correct: includes all and only true statements.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 1.

sub: Medial temporal lobe injury and new learning
stem: After bilateral medial temporal lobe injury, a patient can hold a short conversation but repeatedly fails to recall new ward events after a delay. Remote autobiographical knowledge and a practiced motor skill are relatively better preserved. What is the most appropriate initial interpretation?

options.text: A selective inability to remember only events from before the injury: retrograde amnesia.
A definite loss of all short-term storage.
A pattern consistent with anterograde episodic-memory impairment; testing is needed to separate encoding, consolidation and retrieval contributions.
Proof that all procedural learning and semantic knowledge have been erased.

why: The principal complaint concerns events after injury, consistent with anterograde episodic-memory impairment associated with medial temporal structures. Preserved conversation and skill illustrate relative dissociations, not proof of intact functioning in every task. Additional testing is required to assess specific processes.

optWhy.A: A reverses the temporal definition.
optWhy.B: B is not implied by the preserved conversation or described delay.
optWhy.C: C correctly identifies the temporal pattern and limits inference.
optWhy.D: D contradicts the relatively preserved skill and knowledge.

stem: A cue has been linked to several similar responses in different learning episodes. At test, an incorrect response repeatedly comes to mind and makes the desired response hard to produce. Which account best fits without assuming the target trace has been erased?

options.text: Response competition among associations sharing a cue.
An obligatory failure to perceive the cue.
Complete loss of every association involving the cue.
Anterograde amnesia caused by hippocampal injury.

why: Associative and retrieval competition can impair access when a cue activates multiple candidates. Similarity and contextual overlap often influence competition, but the observation alone does not prove a particular inhibitory or unlearning mechanism.

optWhy.A: A accounts for the intrusive alternative without requiring erasure.
optWhy.B: B is not implied: the cue can be perceived while responses compete.
optWhy.C: C contradicts the generation of an associated response and assumes erasure.
optWhy.D: D invents a neurological diagnosis from a common retrieval difficulty.

stem: Match each observation with the most directly supported description.
why: Cue-supported recovery indicates a retrieval-accessibility problem; endorsing an unstudied lure is false recognition; attributing a correct detail to the wrong origin is a source error; interference arising during output is output interference. None alone identifies every underlying mechanism.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 matches c, not a; 2 matches a, not b; 3 matches d, not c; 4 matches b, not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 matches c, not d; 2 matches a, not c; 3 matches d, not b; 4 matches b, not a.
optWhy.C: Correct: 1–c, 2–a, 3–d, 4–b.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 2 matches a, not b; 4 matches b, not a.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A decline in measured performance across retention intervals does not by itself establish that the stored representation has decayed solely because time elapsed.
reason: Activities and contextual changes that covary with the interval can contribute to memory performance at test.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: Both statements are true. The reason explains why a time trend is insufficient to isolate time-dependent trace decay: differences in intervening activity and test context provide alternative causal accounts. Even controlled intervals do not remove every unobserved process.

optWhy.A: A correctly relates correlated interval factors to the inferential limit.
optWhy.B: B overlooks the explanatory relationship.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly denies the possible contributions of interval activities and context.
optWhy.D: D wrongly treats a time trend as unique proof of decay.

stem: After each word, participants see a random remember or forget instruction. At an unexpected final test they are asked to recall all words; remember-cued words are recalled more often. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The difference proves that forget-cued words were never perceived.
The pattern is directed forgetting and can reflect differential rehearsal or encoding, among other processes; it does not demonstrate unconscious repression.
The pattern shows that all forget-cued words were permanently erased.
The instruction guarantees that participants intentionally retrieved every forget-cued word during study.

why: Better memory for remember-cued than forget-cued items is an item-method directed-forgetting effect. Selective rehearsal and encoding can contribute, and retrieval factors may also matter. An explicit experimental instruction is not equivalent to Freudian unconscious repression.

optWhy.A: A infers absence of perception without measuring it.
optWhy.B: B correctly identifies the effect and limits its mechanism.
optWhy.C: C asserts permanent erasure beyond the data.
optWhy.D: D contradicts the instruction and is not measured.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true for environmental context. 2 is true for state matching. 3 is true: mood congruence is an item-valence relationship, distinct from mood-dependent matching. 4 is false: external and internal context effects can interact but are not identical.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Correct: includes all and only true statements.

key: Separating contextual and affective retrieval effects

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A witness can remember a real event while misremembering a detail introduced after it.
reason: A confidently reported detail must have originated in the witnessed event rather than in a later conversation.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true: post-event information can influence reconstructed details. The reason is false: confidence does not identify the source or guarantee accuracy; a source-monitoring error or other bias is possible.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly treats confidence as proof of source.
optWhy.B: B also accepts the false reason.
optWhy.C: C correctly separates distortion from source certainty.
optWhy.D: D reverses the truth values.

stem: Witnesses see a video containing a blue delivery van. Later, a randomly assigned misleading account describes the van as green; a neutral account does not mention its colour. On a final test, the misleading group reports green more often. Which conclusion best fits?

options.text: Post-event information influenced reports, but response compliance, source confusion and altered memory representations need further controls to distinguish them.
The original blue representation was certainly erased in every participant.
The misleading account proves that the witnesses never saw the van.
Only time-dependent decay can explain the between-group difference.

why: Random assignment supports an effect of the post-event account on subsequent reports. The result is compatible with misinformation and source confusion, but does not establish irreversible overwriting: demand characteristics, response bias and residual access to the original detail need separate tests.

optWhy.A: A identifies the experimental effect without overclaiming its mechanism.
optWhy.B: B asserts universal erasure not demonstrated by reports.
optWhy.C: C confuses a later report with initial perception.
optWhy.D: D ignores the manipulated post-event information.

stem: Match each description with the most appropriate term.
why: Pre-injury memory impairment is retrograde; impaired new learning is anterograde; relatively rapid post-learning molecular stabilisation is synaptic consolidation; restabilisation after suitable reactivation is reconsolidation. A temporal gradient in retrograde amnesia can occur but is neither universal nor sufficient to localise every trace.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 matches d, not a; 3 matches a, not c; 4 matches c, not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 2 matches b, not c; 3 matches a, not b; 4 matches c, not a.
optWhy.C: Correct: 1–d, 2–b, 3–a, 4–c.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 matches d, not b; 2 matches b, not a; 3 matches a, not d.

stem: A witness omits a detail in one account but later states an incorrect colour for the same object. Which distinction best describes these two errors?

options.text: The omission is a retrieval failure or other loss of report; the incorrect colour is a distortion, not simply an omission.
Both necessarily prove that the entire event was never encoded.
Both are examples of anterograde amnesia.
The incorrect colour proves the witness is deliberately lying.

why: An omission is an absence from the report whose cause remains to be established; an incorrect reported feature is a distortion. Either can arise through multiple encoding, storage, retrieval or social processes.

optWhy.A: A distinguishes absence from inaccurate content without assuming a cause.
optWhy.B: B overgeneralises from two errors to total encoding failure.
optWhy.C: C invents a neurological syndrome.
optWhy.D: D infers deliberate deception from an inaccurate memory.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true of Bartlett’s reconstructive account. 2 is true: changes in reporting have multiple possible mechanisms. 3 is false: confidence and vividness do not guarantee accuracy or stability. 4 is true: a co-witness can supply information later misattributed to the event.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Correct: includes all and only true statements.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 1.

stem: A witness sees a plain entrance in a video and later hears another person mention a red sign. At test, the witness confidently reports having seen the sign in the video. A neutral-control witness who did not hear about the sign does not report it. What explanation best fits the first witness’s error?

options.text: The witness necessarily forgot all information about the entrance.
The confident report establishes that a red sign appeared in the video.
Anterograde amnesia prevents the witness from hearing post-event information.
The witness may have remembered the sign from the later account but misattributed its source to the video.

why: The witness reports a detail introduced later as though it had been visually witnessed, consistent with source misattribution and misinformation. The neutral control supports a possible influence of post-event exposure, but one comparison does not establish the mechanism or exclude deliberate responding. Confidence does not verify source accuracy.

optWhy.A: A wrongly equates one added detail with complete forgetting of the event.
optWhy.B: B treats confidence as proof despite the stipulated video.
optWhy.C: C invents an amnesia diagnosis and contradicts the ability to report the detail.
optWhy.D: D identifies the source confusion while allowing alternative explanations.

stem: A shared edge in a reversible silhouette remains physically unchanged, but which adjoining region appears shaped by that edge changes across perceptual reversals. What follows?

options.text: The edge must have moved on the retina.
The visual system must have lost sensitivity to the edge.
Figure assignment and border ownership can change without a change in the shared local contour.
Both regions necessarily become independent foreground objects.

why: In figure–ground organisation, a shared border can be experienced as belonging to one region or the other. A reversal with fixed local input illustrates a change in interpretation, not retinal edge movement or loss of sensitivity.

optWhy.A: A confuses perceptual reversal with physical motion.
optWhy.B: B is not entailed by the unchanged, visible edge.
optWhy.C: C distinguishes border assignment from the local image.
optWhy.D: D is not the stated figure–ground reversal.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A Gestalt grouping description does not by itself specify the neural computation that produces a given grouping.
reason: Symmetry can bias which region is perceived as figure in some displays.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true: a descriptive grouping regularity requires additional mechanistic specification. The reason is also true as a qualified figure–ground tendency, but it does not explain why a Gestalt description alone leaves neural implementation unspecified.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly makes symmetry bias the explanation of the mechanistic gap.
optWhy.B: B correctly identifies both statements as true but non-explanatory.
optWhy.C: C wrongly denies a qualified symmetry effect.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly claims that a grouping description uniquely specifies a neural mechanism.

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: The manipulations isolate, respectively, spacing, similarity, connections and relative motion as candidate influences. Even with these controls, adding a bridge changes local image structure, so interpretation benefits from appropriate visual controls.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Tests whether proximity affects grouping), not a; 2 should match d (Tests whether similarity of features affects grouping), not b; 4 should match a (Tests whether common motion supports grouping), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 2 should match d (Tests whether similarity of features affects grouping), not a; 3 should match c (Tests whether connecting elements alters grouping), not d; 4 should match a (Tests whether common motion supports grouping), not c.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Tests whether proximity affects grouping), not d; 2 should match d (Tests whether similarity of features affects grouping), not c; 3 should match c (Tests whether connecting elements alters grouping), not b.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–b (Alter spacing while holding feature values fixed: Tests whether proximity affects grouping); 2–d (Alter feature similarity while holding locations fixed: Tests whether similarity of features affects grouping); 3–c (Add bridging contours while holding element centres fixed: Tests whether connecting elements alters grouping); 4–a (Change relative motion vectors while holding initial positions fixed: Tests whether common motion supports grouping).

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true as a qualified grouping tendency. 2 is true: grouping cues can conflict. 3 is true for ambiguous figures. 4 is false: perceptual interpretation can reflect both stimulus structure and knowledge or task context.

optWhy.A: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 3.

stem: Observers view noisy fragments that can form either a symmetric shape or an asymmetric alternative. A researcher claims that symmetry itself drives the grouping, rather than differences in local contrast or response preference. Which follow-up best addresses this claim?

options.text: Compare the original display with a brighter version and ask for recognition accuracy alone.
Tell one group the expected answer and compare it with an uninstructed group.
Test only displays in which symmetry and contrast both increase together.
Independently vary global symmetry and local contrast, counterbalance response labels, and measure grouping across several noise levels.

why: A factorial manipulation separates the contribution of symmetry from local contrast; counterbalancing response labels reduces a decision-label confound, and multiple noise levels test robustness under degradation. The design supports a causal test of the manipulated properties, but does not identify a unique neural mechanism.

optWhy.A: A changes brightness without independently manipulating symmetry and measures recognition rather than grouping alone.
optWhy.B: B introduces expectancy differences without separating visual properties.
optWhy.C: C confounds the two candidate influences.
optWhy.D: D independently varies candidate causes and controls response labels.

key: Testing global grouping against local and decision alternatives

stem: A dot lattice is adjusted so proximity favours rows and feature similarity favours columns. As relative spacing changes, the proportion of row reports changes smoothly rather than abruptly. Which interpretation is most useful?

options.text: Prägnanz gives an exact numerical prediction without any additional assumptions.
Competing grouping tendencies can be studied with a psychometric function; a smooth trade-off does not establish a universal cue hierarchy.
The change in reports proves that similarity has no influence.
A perceptual organisation cannot be described probabilistically.

why: A psychometric function relating spacing to reported organisation makes competition measurable. The result can be consistent with graded cue combination, but the relative weights must be estimated; a general appeal to simplicity does not specify exact probabilities or a universal hierarchy.

optWhy.A: A attributes a precise quantitative rule to a broad principle without specifying a model.
optWhy.B: B uses measurable cue competition and avoids a fixed hierarchy.
optWhy.C: C excludes an influence not isolated by the stated observation.
optWhy.D: D wrongly excludes probabilistic descriptions.

stem: A stereoscopic headset displays a simulated object at a near depth, but both images are physically focused on screens at a fixed optical distance. Which conflict can arise?

options.text: Vergence can signal the simulated depth while accommodation is driven by the screen’s optical distance.
Accommodation and vergence must specify identical distances in every display.
The fixed screen removes all binocular disparity between the eye images.
The apparent depth requires texture gradients rather than stereoscopic disparity.

why: A stereoscopic display can vary binocular disparities and the vergence demand associated with virtual depth while the optical focus remains at the screen distance. The resulting vergence–accommodation conflict depends on display and viewing conditions; it does not imply that binocular depth is absent.

optWhy.A: A correctly identifies the distinct depth and optical-focus demands.
optWhy.B: B assumes the coupling cannot be disrupted by a display.
optWhy.C: C ignores the separate eye images that can contain disparity.
optWhy.D: D wrongly makes a monocular texture cue necessary.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: During lateral self-motion, relative image motion can provide information about relative depth when appropriate motion and eye-movement information is available.
reason: Binocular disparity is calculated from positional differences between corresponding features in the two eyes’ images.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true as a qualified description of motion parallax. The reason is also true of binocular disparity, but two-eye correspondence does not explain why lateral self-motion supplies relative-motion depth information. Both are distinct sources of depth information.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly treats a binocular-cue description as the explanation for motion parallax.
optWhy.B: B correctly judges the statements true but non-explanatory.
optWhy.C: C wrongly denies binocular positional differences.
optWhy.D: D wrongly denies the possible depth information from self-motion.

sub: Visual cliff: perceptual and action inference
stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: An infant’s refusal to cross the deep side of a visual cliff, considered alone, proves that fully developed depth perception was present at birth and unaffected by experience.
reason: Avoidance depends on factors such as locomotor ability and wariness in addition to detecting the depth difference.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is false: testing mobile infants does not establish complete innate depth perception or exclude experiential contributions. The reason is true: refusal is an action measure influenced by perceptual, motor and affective factors; complementary measures are needed to study detection in non-crawlers.

optWhy.A: A wrongly accepts the strong developmental claim.
optWhy.B: B also accepts the unsupported assertion.
optWhy.C: C reverses the truth values.
optWhy.D: D correctly separates perceptual discrimination from locomotor avoidance.

key: Limits of avoidance as a measure of infant depth perception

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: A rotating wire object can produce kinetic depth; lateral translation produces motion parallax; pure forward translation creates an expansion field whose focus can indicate heading; paired eye views provide disparity. Real movement and eye rotation can complicate these idealised relationships.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match c (Kinetic depth from changing projected object structure), not a; 2 should match d (Motion parallax with depth-related relative image velocities), not b; 3 should match b (Radial optic flow that can specify heading), not c; 4 should match a (Stereoscopic disparity information), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 should match c (Kinetic depth from changing projected object structure), not b; 2 should match d (Motion parallax with depth-related relative image velocities), not a; 3 should match b (Radial optic flow that can specify heading), not d; 4 should match a (Stereoscopic disparity information), not c.
optWhy.C: Correct: 1–c (Rotate a wire object while a single stationary eye views it: Kinetic depth from changing projected object structure); 2–d (Translate the observer sideways past stationary near and far landmarks: Motion parallax with depth-related relative image velocities); 3–b (Move forward through a static environment with no eye rotation: Radial optic flow that can specify heading); 4–a (Compare relative positions of matched features across the two eyes: Stereoscopic disparity information).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 should match c (Kinetic depth from changing projected object structure), not d; 2 should match d (Motion parallax with depth-related relative image velocities), not c.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: relative disparity supplies relative depth, while metric interpretation requires additional information. 2 is true: one eye can accommodate. 3 is true in displays that separate simulated binocular depth from optical focus. 4 is false: interposition primarily gives ordinal depth, while relative size and texture gradients depend on scene assumptions. Linear perspective, relative height and light–shadow cues likewise provide contextual depth information rather than guaranteed metric distance.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.B: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 3.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4 and omits true statement(s) 1.

key: Ordinal, relative and absolute depth information

stem: In a simulated driving study, a stationary textured environment is viewed during straight-line translation in a direction that may be off-centre; the virtual camera and eyes do not rotate. The radial flow field expands around a point to the right of screen centre. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: The expansion point gives the exact distance to every surface.
The driver’s physical head must be turning to the left.
The scene is necessarily moving towards the observer as a rigid object.
Under these idealised conditions, the expansion centre indicates the direction of translation; extra information is needed when eye or camera rotation is added.

why: For pure translation through a stationary scene, the focus of expansion specifies heading direction, subject to the display’s geometry. Rotational flow from eye or camera movements complicates this simple interpretation, and flow direction alone does not fix absolute distances.

optWhy.A: A attributes metric distance information to the expansion centre alone.
optWhy.B: B infers physical head rotation that is neither required nor established by the virtual geometry.
optWhy.C: C substitutes rigid-object motion for the given observer translation.
optWhy.D: D correctly limits the heading inference to the stated geometry.

stem: Two clinics use a test with hit rate 0.80 and false-alarm rate 0.10. Disease prevalence is 1% in Clinic X and 20% in Clinic Y. Assuming these rates apply in both clinics, approximately what proportion of positive results are true cases in X and Y respectively?
why: Positive predictive value is P(signal|positive) = (prevalence×hit rate) / [prevalence×hit rate + (1−prevalence)×false-alarm rate]. X: 0.008/(0.008+0.099)≈0.075; Y: 0.16/(0.16+0.08)=0.667. Equal conditional hit and false-alarm rates need not yield equal predictive values.

optWhy.A: A correctly combines conditional rates with each base rate.
optWhy.B: B mistakes sensitivity for the probability of disease given a positive.
optWhy.C: C substitutes prevalence or false-alarm rates for predictive value.
optWhy.D: D does not use the stated base-rate-weighted counts.

key: Base rates versus conditional detection rates

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: The difference z(hit rate) − z(false-alarm rate) can change across criteria even if the underlying unequal-variance Gaussian evidence distributions stay fixed.
reason: For unequal-variance Gaussian evidence, a z-ROC with z(hit rate) on the vertical axis and z(false-alarm rate) on the horizontal axis must have slope 1.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true: under unequal variances, this difference can vary with the operating criterion. The reason is false: in the stated axes, the Gaussian z-ROC slope is σnoise/σsignal, and equals one only when the standard deviations are equal.

optWhy.A: A wrongly accepts a universal unit slope.
optWhy.B: B also treats the false reason as true.
optWhy.C: C correctly identifies criterion dependence and the false unit-slope claim.
optWhy.D: D reverses the truth values.

key: Criterion dependence of d′ under unequal variances

stem: Relative to baseline H=0.6915 and F=0.3085, match each condition in List-I with its change in List-II. Assume equal-variance Gaussian yes/no SDT, d′=z(H)−z(F), c=−[z(H)+z(F)]/2, and lower c means more liberal. Use z(0.1587)=−1, z(0.3085)=−0.5, z(0.5000)=0, z(0.6915)=0.5, z(0.8413)=1.
why: Use the baseline H=0.6915, F=0.3085, d′=1 and c=0. P has d′=1, c=−0.5; Q has d′=1, c=0.5; R has d′=2, c=0; S has d′=0, c=0. A lower c indicates a more liberal criterion in this convention.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match c (Same sensitivity as baseline; more liberal criterion), not a; 2 should match a (Same sensitivity as baseline; more conservative criterion), not b; 3 should match b (Greater sensitivity than baseline; same criterion), not c.
optWhy.B: Correct: 1–c (Condition P: H=0.8413, F=0.5000: Same sensitivity as baseline; more liberal criterion); 2–a (Condition Q: H=0.5000, F=0.1587: Same sensitivity as baseline; more conservative criterion); 3–b (Condition R: H=0.8413, F=0.1587: Greater sensitivity than baseline; same criterion); 4–d (Condition S: H=0.5000, F=0.5000: Lower sensitivity than baseline; same criterion).
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 should match c (Same sensitivity as baseline; more liberal criterion), not b; 3 should match b (Greater sensitivity than baseline; same criterion), not d; 4 should match d (Lower sensitivity than baseline; same criterion), not c.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 should match c (Same sensitivity as baseline; more liberal criterion), not d; 2 should match a (Same sensitivity as baseline; more conservative criterion), not c; 4 should match d (Lower sensitivity than baseline; same criterion), not a.

stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: A chance-diagonal ROC has chance discrimination. Crossing curves do not support blanket dominance across all criteria. Under the stated tie-free scoring assumptions, AUC is the probability that signal evidence exceeds noise evidence. A move along one fixed ROC can reflect a criterion change with the underlying distributions fixed.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match d (Chance-level discrimination under the plotted measure), not a; 4 should match a (A change in operating criterion without requiring a change in the fixed evidence distributions), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 should match d (Chance-level discrimination under the plotted measure), not b; 2 should match b (No single curve dominates at every operating point), not a; 3 should match c (Probability is 0.80 that a randomly sampled signal receives a higher evidence score than a randomly sampled noise trial), not d; 4 should match a (A change in operating criterion without requiring a change in the fixed evidence distributions), not c.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 2 should match b (No single curve dominates at every operating point), not c; 3 should match c (Probability is 0.80 that a randomly sampled signal receives a higher evidence score than a randomly sampled noise trial), not b.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–d (ROC entirely on the chance diagonal: Chance-level discrimination under the plotted measure); 2–b (Two empirical ROC curves cross: No single curve dominates at every operating point); 3–c (Area under a tie-free ROC is 0.80: Probability is 0.80 that a randomly sampled signal receives a higher evidence score than a randomly sampled noise trial); 4–a (Move along a fixed ROC towards a higher false-alarm rate: A change in operating criterion without requiring a change in the fixed evidence distributions).

key: Interpreting ROC shape, AUC and operating points

sub: Conditional SDT outcomes and decision costs
stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: the rates have different denominators. 2 is true: rewards and costs can influence criterion. 3 is false: raw counts alone lack denominators and false-alarm information. 4 is true: lowering the threshold generally increases both conditional yes rates with fixed distributions.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.

sub: Numerical SDT: sensitivity with equal criteria
stem: Two radiologists each assess 10,000 signal-present and 10,000 signal-absent scans. A has 6,915 hits and 3,085 false alarms; B has 9,332 hits and 668 false alarms. Assume equal-variance Gaussian yes/no SDT. Use z(0.6915)=0.5, z(0.3085)=−0.5, z(0.9332)=1.5 and z(0.0668)=−1.5; d′=z(H)−z(F), c=−[z(H)+z(F)]/2. Which result follows?

options.text: Both have d′=1, but B has a more liberal criterion.
Both have d′=3, but B has a more conservative criterion.

why: A has H=0.6915 and F=0.3085, so d′=0.5−(−0.5)=1 and c=0. B has H=0.9332 and F=0.0668, so d′=1.5−(−1.5)=3 and c=0. Under the stipulated model B has higher sensitivity with equal c; sampling uncertainty is not addressed by the point estimates.

optWhy.A: A correctly computes both sensitivity and midpoint criteria.
optWhy.B: B reverses the sensitivity estimates.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly treats the sensitivity estimates as equal.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly assigns equal d′ and different criteria.

key: Numerical separation of sensitivity and bias

stem: A matte white card is moved from daylight into dim shade. Its luminance reaching the eye falls substantially, yet observers still judge it to be white. Which distinction best describes this observation?

options.text: Brightness is identical to reflectance and cannot change with illumination.
Approximate lightness constancy can coexist with a change in perceived brightness because lightness concerns apparent surface reflectance.
The card must emit the same luminance in both locations.
The observed stability proves the visual system measures physical reflectance independently of context.

why: Lightness concerns the apparent light–dark surface property, often related to reflectance; brightness concerns apparent intensity of light from a region. Changing illumination can alter luminance and brightness while lightness remains relatively stable, depending on context and viewing conditions.

optWhy.A: A conflates brightness with surface lightness.
optWhy.B: B correctly separates apparent surface property from light intensity.
optWhy.C: C contradicts the stipulated change in luminance.
optWhy.D: D claims context-independent measurement that the example does not establish.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A fixed-angular-size afterimage can appear larger when viewed against a surface perceived as more distant.
reason: In size–distance scaling, perceived size for a fixed visual angle increases with perceived distance.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true as an Emmert-type observation. The reason is true and explains it: holding angular extent fixed, a larger perceived projection distance yields a larger perceived size in the scaling account. The relation is approximate and depends on available distance cues.

optWhy.A: A correctly relates fixed angular size to distance scaling.
optWhy.B: B overlooks the explanatory relation.
optWhy.C: C wrongly rejects the stated scaling relation.
optWhy.D: D wrongly denies the qualified afterimage effect.

sub: Types of constancy under specific changes
stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: Distance can alter image size without an equivalent change in perceived physical size; slant changes projection while shape may remain stable; lightness and colour constancy concern surface appearance under intensity and spectral changes. All are graded and depend on scene information.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Approximately stable perceived physical size), not a; 2 should match c (Approximately stable perceived shape despite changes in projection), not b; 3 should match d (Approximately stable perceived surface lightness despite changed luminance), not c; 4 should match a (Approximately stable perceived surface colour), not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 2 should match c (Approximately stable perceived shape despite changes in projection), not a; 4 should match a (Approximately stable perceived surface colour), not c.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 should match b (Approximately stable perceived physical size), not d; 3 should match d (Approximately stable perceived surface lightness despite changed luminance), not b.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–b (Same object moved farther with distance cues available: Approximately stable perceived physical size); 2–c (Same door viewed at different slants: Approximately stable perceived shape despite changes in projection); 3–d (Same achromatic surface moved between bright and dim neutral illumination: Approximately stable perceived surface lightness despite changed luminance); 4–a (Same coloured surface viewed under different spectral illuminants: Approximately stable perceived surface colour).

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: the light reaching the eye depends on illumination and reflectance. 2 is true: adaptation and contextual comparisons can contribute. 3 is false: one receptor response under narrow-band light underdetermines the full reflectance spectrum. 4 is true: constancy depends on information and need not be perfect.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: projection and perceived shape need not match. 2 is true: less reliable distance information can reduce compensation. 3 is false: fixed angle with differing perceived distances can yield differing apparent sizes. 4 is true: perspective interpretations can influence size judgments, though individual illusion mechanisms require testing.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2.

stem: Two physically identical grey test patches each have luminance 20 units. One is embedded in a region averaging 80 units; the other is embedded in a region averaging 20 units. Observers judge the patches differently in lightness. Which follow-up best separates a local luminance-ratio account from an interpretation based on perceived illumination?

options.text: Independently manipulate surrounding luminance and cues to illumination while keeping test-patch luminance fixed.
Change patch luminance and shadow geometry together and compare mean reports.
Ask observers which patch is objectively brighter without measuring the display.
Remove all comparison conditions and retain only the original image.

why: A factorial design with fixed test-patch luminance can test whether judgments track local ratios, illumination cues, or their interaction. Both accounts can predict context effects; the original comparison alone does not establish which mechanism caused the difference.

optWhy.A: A independently varies the competing explanatory cues.
optWhy.B: B confounds the two factors of interest.
optWhy.C: C replaces controlled measurements with a single uncalibrated judgment.
optWhy.D: D provides no basis for separating the explanations.

stem: After orientation-discrimination training at one visual-field location, performance rises there but transfers weakly to an untrained location. What additional observation would best support a location-specific sensitivity change rather than only a shift in response preference?

options.text: More correct responses at the trained location without any error analysis.
Greater confidence at the trained location with no signal-absent trials.
A preference for one response label after training.
An increased trained-location ROC with suitable pre/post controls, while the untrained-location ROC changes little.

why: A higher ROC across operating criteria at the trained location, relative to an appropriately controlled untrained location, supports a location-specific change in discrimination beyond one response threshold. Such specificity does not by itself localise plasticity exclusively to early visual cortex.

optWhy.A: A omits false alarms and response preferences.
optWhy.B: B provides insufficient evidence to distinguish confidence from discrimination.
optWhy.C: C is evidence of preference rather than necessarily better sensitivity.
optWhy.D: D uses criterion-independent comparisons while testing transfer.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A higher hit rate after an expectancy cue does not by itself establish improved perceptual sensitivity.
reason: Expectancy may shift a response criterion and thereby increase both hit and false-alarm rates even if evidence distributions remain unchanged.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is true because hit rate alone confounds discrimination and criterion. The reason is true and directly explains how expectancy can increase hits without improving the separation of signal and noise. A design should measure both trial types and compare sensitivity.

optWhy.A: A correctly explains the ambiguity using a criterion shift.
optWhy.B: B ignores the explanatory relation.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly denies the possible criterion effect.
optWhy.D: D wrongly treats hit rate alone as sufficient to establish sensitivity.

sub: Integrating cognitive processes and experimental controls
stem: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct code.
why: Location-specific training can be assessed with sensitivity and transfer tests; encoding specificity requires matched cue comparisons; dual-task interference requires baseline performance; operant attention allocation requires measuring how contingent feedback changes future behaviour.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 2 should match b (compare reinstated and changed retrieval cues), not c; 3 should match c (compare dual-task costs with single-task baselines), not b.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 should match a (Assess sensitivity and transfer across trained and untrained locations), not b; 2 should match b (Compare retrieval when encoded cues are reinstated versus changed), not a; 3 should match c (Compare dual-task costs with matched single-task baselines), not d; 4 should match d (Test whether feedback changes future allocation of looking), not c.
optWhy.C: Correct: 1–a (Orientation discrimination after training: Assess sensitivity and transfer across trained and untrained locations); 2–b (Remembering an event with a reinstated study cue: Compare retrieval when encoded cues are reinstated versus changed); 3–c (Visual search while holding spatial locations in mind: Compare dual-task costs with matched single-task baselines); 4–d (Looking towards a region followed by contingent feedback: Test whether feedback changes future allocation of looking).
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 should match a (Assess sensitivity and transfer across trained and untrained locations), not d; 2 should match b (Compare retrieval when encoded cues are reinstated versus changed), not c; 3 should match c (Compare dual-task costs with matched single-task baselines), not b; 4 should match d (Test whether feedback changes future allocation of looking), not a.

key: Matching integrative claims to discriminating tests

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: shared resources are a possible explanation but not uniquely established by a dual-task cost. 2 is true: single-task baselines help interpret divided-performance costs. 3 is false: specificity alone does not uniquely localise the change. 4 is true: feedback effects on attention require analysis of actual contingent behaviour.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3 and omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Correct: selects all and only true statements 1, 2, 4.

key: Limits of inference from load and training specificity

sub: Working memory, attention and perceptual sensitivity
stem: Participants detect a faint tilted grating in noise while maintaining either spatial locations or spoken digits. Spatial load produces more errors. The researcher claims a specific visual-sensitivity loss. Which additional design best tests that claim?

options.text: Compare only average confidence between load conditions.
Measure full hit and false-alarm functions across several response criteria, match single-task difficulty, and monitor eye position in both load conditions.
Increase the spatial load while simultaneously reducing stimulus contrast.
Exclude false alarms and analyse only correct signal-present trials.

why: Comparing ROCs across load conditions helps distinguish sensitivity from criterion changes. Single-task baselines and eye tracking address difficulty and fixation confounds. If ROCs differ, alternative changes in attention or encoding still require investigation; a result need not prove a unique storage module.

optWhy.A: A does not separate confidence, criterion and discrimination.
optWhy.B: B provides both criterion-sensitive data and important task controls.
optWhy.C: C confounds load with physical stimulus quality.
optWhy.D: D omits the false-alarm information needed for SDT.

key: Disentangling load, fixation and perceptual sensitivity

stem: A previously neutral tone predicts an aversive event after conditioning. On a separate visual detection task, tone and no-tone blocks have H and F respectively: tone (0.9332, 0.6915), no tone (0.8413, 0.5000). Assume equal-variance Gaussian SDT and fixed evidence distributions; z(0.9332)=1.5, z(0.6915)=0.5, z(0.8413)=1 and z(0.5000)=0. With d′=z(H)−z(F) and c=−[z(H)+z(F)]/2, which interpretation fits?

options.text: Tone d′=2 and no-tone d′=1, with equal c.
Tone d′=1 and no-tone d′=2, with equal c.
Both d′ values are 1; c shifts from −0.5 without tone to −1.0 with tone, consistent with a more liberal criterion.
Both d′ values are 1; c shifts from −1.0 without tone to −0.5 with tone, consistent with a more conservative criterion.

why: Tone: d′=1.5−0.5=1 and c=−(1.5+0.5)/2=−1. No tone: d′=1−0=1 and c=−(1+0)/2=−0.5. With the stipulated equal-variance model, the tone condition has a more liberal criterion without a point-estimate change in d′. Conditioning could affect expectation or arousal, but these data alone do not identify which psychological pathway caused the shift.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly computes tone sensitivity.
optWhy.B: B incorrectly computes no-tone sensitivity.
optWhy.C: C correctly calculates both indices and limits the causal interpretation.
optWhy.D: D reverses the criterion values and direction.

key: Conditioned cue, expectation and detection bias

stem: A student keeps looking at a textbook while a sudden sound to the left automatically draws attention there, without an eye movement. Which description applies?
why: The sound triggers exogenous orienting; because gaze stays fixed, the shift is covert. Endogenous orienting is voluntary or goal-directed, and overt orienting involves a gaze shift.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly describes both the trigger and gaze.
optWhy.B: B correctly identifies stimulus-driven attention without gaze movement.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly describes the trigger as voluntary.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly requires an eye movement.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A reduction in a conditioned response during extinction does not by itself establish permanent erasure of the original association.
reason: A conditioned response can reappear after a delay without new pairings, as in spontaneous recovery.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: Both are true; recovery supports the claim that low extinction performance does not prove permanent erasure. Recovery need not mean extinction learning has vanished.

optWhy.A: A correctly links recovery with the limitation of an erasure inference.
optWhy.B: B ignores the explanatory link.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly denies spontaneous recovery.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly asserts that extinction performance proves erasure.

stem: Match each task demand with the working-memory component most directly implicated, not necessarily the only component involved.
why: The loop maintains verbal sound, the sketchpad supports spatial representations, the executive coordinates tasks, and the episodic buffer integrates information. These are functional constructs, not mutually exclusive brain areas.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 2 matches d, not a; 3 matches a, not c; 4 matches c, not d.
optWhy.B: Correct: 1–b, 2–d, 3–a, 4–c.
