optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not d; 2 matches d, not c; 4 matches c, not b.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: cues can compete. 2 is true: closure and continuation can differ in their preferred completion. 3 is true as a qualified grouping tendency. 4 is false: simplicity needs an operational model for precise prediction.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.C: Correct: includes all and only true statements.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 2.

stem: During an hour-long monitoring task, early trials yield H=0.8413 and F=0.1587; late trials yield H=0.6915 and F=0.3085. Under equal-variance Gaussian yes/no SDT, use z(0.8413)=1, z(0.1587)=−1, z(0.6915)=0.5 and z(0.3085)=−0.5; d′=z(H)−z(F) and c=−[z(H)+z(F)]/2. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: d′ decreases from 2 to 1; c remains 0.
d′ stays 2; c becomes more liberal.
d′ rises from 1 to 2; c remains 0.
d′ stays 1; c becomes more conservative.

why: Early d′=1−(−1)=2 and c=0. Late d′=0.5−(−0.5)=1 and c=0. The point estimates suggest a vigilance-related sensitivity decrement, not a criterion shift; uncertainty and time-related confounds still need evaluation. ROC measurements at multiple criteria could test the assumed distributional account.

optWhy.A: A correctly calculates both measures.
optWhy.B: B mistakes a reduction in separation for a criterion shift.
optWhy.C: C reverses the estimated change.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly makes sensitivity constant and criterion change.

stem: After training on a mirror-tracing task, a person with severe episodic amnesia improves across days while denying any recollection of practice. Which inference is best?

options.text: Successful skill learning always requires conscious recollection.
Improved tracing proves normal episodic memory.
The patient must be deliberately concealing recollection.
Procedural improvement can occur without explicit episodic recollection.

why: Skill performance can improve without explicit memory for training episodes. The dissociation does not imply that every implicit skill or every explicit-memory process is intact.

optWhy.A: A is contradicted by the observed dissociation.
optWhy.B: B equates skill improvement with recollection.
optWhy.C: C is an unsupported attribution.
optWhy.D: D correctly distinguishes procedural learning and episodic recollection.

key: Dissociation of procedural and episodic memory

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A person may fail to recall an encoded event with one cue and later recall it with a more effective cue.
reason: Recall can depend on the overlap between retrieval cues and features encoded with the event.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: Both are true, and encoding specificity explains why cue variation can reveal previously inaccessible information. The pattern alone does not prove that the memory trace was completely unchanged.

optWhy.A: A captures the explanatory relation.
optWhy.B: B overlooks that cue overlap explains the difference.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly denies encoding specificity.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly denies cue-dependent recovery.

stem: Match each theoretical position with its characteristic claim, not a finding that uniquely proves it.
why: Broadbent emphasised a physical-characteristic filter; Treisman proposed attenuation with varying thresholds; Deutsch and Deutsch proposed late selection; Norman included pertinence as a determinant of activation. Actual selective-listening findings do not settle all model variants.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not a; 2 matches c, not b; 3 matches a, not c.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not c; 2 matches c, not d; 3 matches a, not b; 4 matches d, not a.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 2 matches c, not a; 3 matches a, not d; 4 matches d, not c.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–b, 2–c, 3–a, 4–d.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: partial report estimates information initially available. 2 is true: the advantage declines with cue delay and masking conditions. 3 is false: visual and auditory sensory persistence differ and depend on procedure. 4 is true: performance cannot by itself isolate encoding from later processes.

optWhy.A: Correct: includes all and only true statements.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 4.

stem: Two groups receive the same number of tone–shock pairings. For Group X, P(shock|tone)=0.40 and P(shock|no tone)=0.05; for Group Y, P(shock|tone)=0.40 and P(shock|no tone)=0.40. Tone and background exposure are matched across groups and all animals receive the same test. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Identical pairing counts require identical conditioned responding in all subjects.
Group Y has the stronger positive contingency because its no-tone shock probability is higher.
Tone–shock temporal contiguity is absent in both groups.
Group X has a more positive contingency; stronger tone conditioning in X would support a predictive-information account, not uniquely prove it.

why: The contingency difference P(shock|tone)−P(shock|no tone) is 0.35 for X and 0 for Y. Both have pairings, but only X’s tone predicts elevated shock probability. A controlled result favouring X supports contingency-sensitive learning while leaving other mechanisms to examine.

optWhy.A: A ignores information from shock outside the tone.
optWhy.B: B reverses the contingency comparison.
optWhy.C: C contradicts the stated paired events.
optWhy.D: D correctly compares conditional probabilities and limits theoretical inference.

stem: When a student presses a button, an aversive tone stops. Button pressing subsequently increases in that situation. Which functional classification is supported?
why: Removing an aversive stimulus following a response, accompanied by an increase in future responding, is negative reinforcement. The label is defined by the consequence and its effect on behaviour, not by whether the event is unpleasant.

optWhy.A: A is incorrect: the stimulus is removed and behaviour increases.
optWhy.B: B is incorrect: punishment reduces future responding.
optWhy.C: C correctly identifies stimulus removal and increased responding.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly describes addition of a stimulus.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Perceived size can remain approximately stable as an object moves farther away despite its smaller retinal projection.
reason: Figure–ground organisation can assign a shared boundary to one region rather than the other.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: Both statements are true. However, figure–ground border assignment is not by itself the explanation of size–distance compensation; the reason is related to perception but logically independent.

optWhy.A: A wrongly treats border ownership as the explanation of size constancy.
optWhy.B: B correctly identifies two true but non-explanatory statements.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly rejects border ownership.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly rejects approximate size constancy.

stem: Match each schedule with its defined contingency, not an invariable response pattern.
why: FR requires a fixed response count; VR a variable count; FI the first response after a fixed interval; VI the first response after a variable interval. Typical rates and pauses vary with procedural details.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not a; 2 matches d, not b; 4 matches a, not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not d; 2 matches d, not c; 3 matches c, not a; 4 matches a, not b.
optWhy.C: Correct: 1–b, 2–d, 3–c, 4–a.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 2 matches d, not a; 3 matches c, not d; 4 matches a, not c.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 and 2 are true and differ in interference direction. 3 is false: competing material and cue accessibility are alternatives to pure time-based decay. 4 is true: Ebbinghaus studied retention and savings, but no single forgetting curve is universal.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Correct: includes all and only true statements.

stem: Two groups hear the same word lists. One recalls immediately; the other counts backwards for 30 seconds before recall. The delayed group shows markedly reduced recency but similar primacy. Which conclusion is warranted?

options.text: The pattern is consistent with a recency contribution vulnerable to the filled delay, but does not uniquely prove a separate short-term store.
The filled delay necessarily erased all long-term traces of final words.
Primacy shows that no rehearsal could have occurred.
The result proves that interference cannot affect memory.

why: A filled delay often reduces immediate recency while leaving primacy less affected. This fits a vulnerable recent-information contribution, but other accounts, including changing distinctiveness and interference, require further tests.

optWhy.A: A gives a qualified interpretation.
optWhy.B: B makes a universal erasure claim unsupported by the result.
optWhy.C: C wrongly excludes rehearsal from primacy.
optWhy.D: D ignores interference as a possible contributor.

key: Serial position and filled retention interval

stem: A pedestrian moves sideways past a stationary scene; near objects shift more rapidly in the retinal image than distant ones. Which additional distinction is most accurate?

options.text: Relative motion specifies exact absolute distance without movement information.
Motion parallax provides relative depth information, whereas optic flow during locomotion can also inform heading under suitable conditions.
Binocular disparity and motion parallax require both eyes simultaneously.
A pictorial occlusion cue specifies the exact metric distance between two surfaces.

why: Motion parallax can support relative depth from motion; optic flow can inform heading, especially under pure translation and suitable viewing geometry. Absolute distance generally needs additional scale information; eye rotation complicates flow interpretation.

optWhy.A: A overstates the information available.
optWhy.B: B correctly distinguishes relative-depth and flow information.
optWhy.C: C wrongly makes parallax binocular.
optWhy.D: D confuses ordinal occlusion with metric distance.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Thorndike’s later law of effect gave reward and punishment equally strong and symmetrical connection-strengthening and weakening effects.
reason: Thorndike initially emphasised both satisfying and annoying consequences but later questioned a symmetrical direct weakening effect of punishment.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion is false and the reason is true. His revision placed greater emphasis on rewarding outcomes, without demonstrating that punishment can never suppress behaviour.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly accepts the symmetry claim.
optWhy.B: B also accepts the false assertion.
optWhy.C: C reverses the truth values.
optWhy.D: D correctly describes the historical revision.

key: Thorndike’s revision of the law of effect

stem: Match the phenomenon to its most direct interpretation; none is assumed to be process-pure.
why: The event is episodic, general factual knowledge semantic, motor skill improvement procedural, and facilitation of degraded-word identification is perceptual priming. Tests can involve multiple processes and are not inherently pure.

optWhy.A: Correct: 1–c, 2–a, 3–d, 4–b.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 matches c, not a; 2 matches a, not b; 3 matches d, not c; 4 matches b, not d.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 matches c, not b; 2 matches a, not d; 3 matches d, not c; 4 matches b, not a.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: 1 matches c, not d; 2 matches a, not c; 3 matches d, not a.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true under appropriate message-switching tests. 2 is true as a challenge to an absolute early-filter claim, although attention shifts and methodological alternatives require control. 3 is false: automaticity is graded and multidimensional. 4 is true: Stroop findings alone do not uniquely locate selection.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Correct: includes all and only true statements.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 3; omits true statement(s) 1.

key: Limits of fixed selection and all-or-none automaticity

stem: Participants learn several category–exemplar pairs, repeatedly retrieve half the exemplars from some categories, and then recall every item. Unpractised exemplars from practised categories are recalled less well than exemplars from entirely unpractised categories. What is the best inference?

options.text: Practice improved all items equally, so no forgetting occurred.
The observed pattern is consistent with retrieval-induced forgetting; baseline matching and independent retrieval cues help test competition or inhibition accounts.
The result uniquely proves unconscious repression.
The result demonstrates that all unpractised items were never encoded.

why: The comparison is the standard retrieval-induced forgetting pattern: related unpractised items are disadvantaged relative to baseline. Item selection, competition and cue dependence should be controlled; independent probes can test whether effects generalise beyond the original retrieval cue.

optWhy.A: A contradicts the relative deficit.
optWhy.B: B states the supported pattern and relevant controls.
optWhy.C: C equates experimental forgetting with a disputed clinical mechanism.
optWhy.D: D assumes an encoding failure not established by the data.

sub: Learning versus performance in historical theories
stem: After equally reinforced maze training, two animals show different test speeds when one is food-deprived and the other is satiated. Which account best distinguishes the theories without treating speed as a direct measure of learning?

options.text: Guthrie required biological drive reduction to form every stimulus–movement association.
Hull equated habit strength with current response speed and excluded motivation.
Thorndike claimed readiness and consequences could not influence behaviour.
Hull distinguished learned habit from drive affecting performance; Guthrie emphasised stimulus–movement contiguity and did not make reinforcement essential for each association.

why: Hull’s drive can influence expression of an established habit; Guthrie emphasised contiguity and one-trial formation of a specific association. Thorndike’s readiness law concerned an organism’s preparedness to act, while later revisions reduced the weight of mere exercise. The speed difference alone cannot measure latent habit.

optWhy.A: A imposes Hull’s drive reduction on Guthrie.
optWhy.B: B collapses a performance outcome into habit and excludes drive.
optWhy.C: C misrepresents readiness and the law of effect.
optWhy.D: D correctly differentiates the historical positions.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: Meaningful elaboration at encoding can improve later memory relative to a shallow task, all else appropriately controlled.
reason: The central executive is one proposed component of working memory.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: Both statements are true. The central executive’s membership in the model does not itself explain why meaningful elaboration can support retention; encoding operations and comparison conditions matter. Organisation and chunking can aid performance, but a chunk count is not a fixed number of raw items.

optWhy.A: A wrongly treats model membership as the causal explanation.
optWhy.B: B correctly identifies both true statements without an explanatory link.
optWhy.C: C incorrectly denies the central executive.
optWhy.D: D incorrectly denies the qualified elaboration effect.

stem: Match each judgement with the physical change it can approximately compensate for.
why: Perceived physical size can remain stable as distance alters projection; perceived shape across angle; lightness across illumination intensity; and colour across changes in spectral illumination. Each depends on available cues and is imperfect. Brightness refers to apparent light intensity, whereas lightness concerns apparent surface reflectance.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not a; 2 matches d, not b; 4 matches a, not d.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 1 matches b, not d; 2 matches d, not b.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 2 matches d, not a; 3 matches c, not d; 4 matches a, not c.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–b, 2–d, 3–c, 4–a.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: different stages can reduce recall. 2 is true: source can be misattributed. 3 is true: reconstructive errors may be confidently held. 4 is false: motivated forgetting and repression are debated and absence of recall cannot establish repression.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 3.
optWhy.B: Correct: includes all and only true statements.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 1.

key: Multiple causes of remembering and forgetting

stem: In a driving simulator, participants steer and classify auditory signals either separately or together. Dual-task performance declines. A second experiment alternates tasks and finds slower responses on switches than repetitions, even after a preparation interval. Which conclusion is defensible?

options.text: A dual-task cost and a switch cost are separately demonstrated; their mechanisms require matched baselines and further tests.
The two costs prove that every task uses one indivisible central resource.
The switch cost is identical by definition to the dual-task cost.
The results prove that controlled processing cannot become more efficient with practice.

why: Comparing simultaneous performance with single-task baselines estimates dual-task costs; comparing switch and repetition trials estimates switch costs. The two measures need not have the same mechanism; order, speed–accuracy trade-offs and task difficulty warrant control.

optWhy.A: A correctly identifies separate operational contrasts and their limits.
optWhy.B: B overgeneralises a single bottleneck from two costs.
optWhy.C: C conflates concurrent performance with changing task sets.
optWhy.D: D makes an unsupported universal claim about practice.

stem: An eyewitness recalls more details when interviewed in a room resembling the original scene. Which alternative must be tested before attributing the difference specifically to context-dependent retrieval?

options.text: The matching room eliminates the possibility of false memories.
The original event was necessarily encoded under divided attention.
Room reinstatement may change mood, expectations, interview behaviour or the cues supplied, rather than only context overlap.
Any benefit demonstrates that the same environmental context is required for recognition.

why: An environmental cue can support retrieval, but reinstating a room can also change mood, expectation and interviewing. State-dependent memory involves match of internal state, whereas context dependence concerns external context; separate manipulation is required to distinguish them.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly rules out reconstruction.
optWhy.B: B asserts an unobserved encoding condition.
optWhy.C: C identifies plausible confounds and a discrimination needed in design.
optWhy.D: D turns a possible benefit into a necessary condition.

stem: Evaluate the assertion and reason using the codes in the options.
assertion: A new stimulus can acquire a conditioned response through pairing with a previously established conditioned stimulus, without direct pairing of the new stimulus with the unconditioned stimulus.
reason: Higher-order conditioning is identical to generalisation because the new stimulus must physically resemble the original conditioned stimulus.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

why: The assertion describes higher-order conditioning. The reason is false: generalisation concerns response to similar stimuli, and physical similarity is not the defining requirement of higher-order conditioning.

optWhy.A: A incorrectly accepts the reason.
optWhy.B: B also treats the false reason as true.
optWhy.C: C correctly distinguishes higher-order conditioning from generalisation.
optWhy.D: D reverses the truth values.

sub: Operant concepts in a sustained-response intervention
stem: Match each intervention or observation with its most precise concept.
why: A differential lamp signals reinforcement availability and can acquire discriminative control; shaping reinforces successive approximations; extinction withholds the previously contingent outcome; partial reinforcement provides the outcome on only some eligible responses. Resistance to extinction often differs with history, but is not universal.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: 1 matches c, not a; 2 matches a, not b; 3 matches b, not c.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: 3 matches b, not d; 4 matches d, not b.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: 1 matches c, not d; 2 matches a, not b; 3 matches b, not c; 4 matches d, not a.
optWhy.D: Correct: 1–c, 2–a, 3–b, 4–d.

stem: Which statements are correct? Select one code.
why: 1 is true: relative disparity does not automatically give absolute metric distance. 2 is true: pictorial cues can work monocularly. 3 is true: grouping may affect recognition without being synonymous with it. 4 is false: illusions may combine image evidence and contextual interpretation, and do not prove an exclusively top-down account.

optWhy.A: Correct: includes all and only true statements.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 2.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 1.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: includes false statement(s) 4; omits true statement(s) 3.

key: Perception as interaction of image and contextual information

sub: Selective attention, encoding and later retrieval
stem: A brief display contains two overlapping scenes. Participants attend one scene at study. At test, unattended-scene items show weak free recall but above-chance forced-choice recognition. Which design and conclusion best discriminate encoding from retrieval accounts?

options.text: Conclude that normal-strength traces were certainly stored and only the retrieval cue failed.
Conclude that every unattended item was fully analysed and consolidated.
Randomly vary study attention while equating exposure, then compare matched recognition and cued-recall tests with control items; the dissociation alone does not isolate the locus.
Repeat only free recall with the same instructions and infer encoding directly.

why: Recognition can outperform free recall because tests differ in cues, decision demands and sensitivity. Randomising attention, holding exposure constant and using controlled tests can constrain encoding versus retrieval explanations, but above-chance recognition does not imply normal encoding or perfect storage.

optWhy.A: A infers intact storage from recognition without measuring trace strength.
optWhy.B: B overstates the degree of unattended encoding.
optWhy.C: C uses manipulated attention and complementary tests while acknowledging limits.
optWhy.D: D fails to distinguish an encoding deficit from a retrieval difficulty.
